A common antibiotic may be linked to a higher risk of miscarriage and stillbirth when used early in pregnancy, a upcoming study suggests.

It has been revealed that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Taking doxycycline, a commonly prescribed antibiotic, during the first trimester of pregnancy may increase the risk of pregnancy loss, a new study suggests.

The antibiotic is broad-spectrum, meaning it targets a wide range of bacteria. It's often used to treat acne, respiratory infections and sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia and syphilis. Doctors generally avoid prescribing the drug during the second and third trimesters because it belongs to a class of antibiotics that can bind to calcium in developing bones. Animal studies suggest that this may disrupt fetal bone development.

Industry observers note that however, evidence on doxycycline's safety during early pregnancy has been mixed and limited. The new study, published Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, provides clearer evidence of a link between doxycycline use in the first trimester and pregnancy loss.

"I would advise physicians to carefully consider the benefit-risk balance when prescribing doxycycline to women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy," study first author Almut Winterstein, a pharmacist and drug-safety researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science in an email.

Using information from two U.S. insurance databases, the researchers analyzed 224,870 pregnancies in people ages 12 to 55. More than 218,230 of these patients were treated for respiratory tract infections, and over 6,630 were treated for acne, between conception and the end of the first trimester. About 4,385 of the women filled a prescription for doxycycline during that time frame, while the others received an alternative antibiotic.

Among women with respiratory infections, those prescribed doxycycline had a 40% to 54% higher risk of pregnancy loss, compared with those prescribed amoxicillin, another broad-spectrum antibiotic in a different class. The exact level of risk varied between the two databases.

Sources indicate that the researchers also compared the doxycycline users against women prescribed macrolides, the class of antibiotics that includes azithromycin (or "Z-Pak"). Again, the doxycycline users saw a higher risk — 39% and 36% higher, respectively.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, among the patients treated for acne, doxycycline customers had a 49% higher risk of pregnancy loss in one database than those given the antibiotic clindamycin. In the second database, though, the difference wasn't statistically significant. Winterstein mentioned that may be because there were fewer patients included in that analysis.

Overall, doxycycline was associated with seven to 11 additional pregnancy losses per 100 pregnancies, compared with the other antibiotic options assessed, the researchers reported.

The researchers examined the risk associated with taking various antibiotics in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

It is not yet clear how the drug might contribute to pregnancy loss. Because the study was observational, it cannot prove that the antibiotic itself caused those losses, which included miscarriages and stillbirths. (Miscarriage is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks of pregnancy, whereas stillbirth refers to pregnancy loss after the 20th week.).

Animal studies hint that doxycycline could interfere with early placental development, potentially making it harder for the placenta to support a growing pregnancy, Luke Grzeskowiak, an associate professor and clinical pharmacist at Flinders University in Australia who was not involved in the study, stated in an email.

It has been revealed that the study authors also noted in their report that the drug may have direct effects on the developing embryo. But these explanations remain hypothetical; the researchers have not established that either mechanism occurs in humans.

Sources indicate that "Pregnancy loss affects around one in four pregnancies and can happen for many reasons," Grzeskowiak noted. Although doxycycline exposure may add to that risk, taking the antibiotic does not necessarily mean pregnancy loss will occur. The available data suggests that it is just one risk factor among many.

Sources indicate that because doxycycline may be prescribed before a pregnancy is recognized, doctors should consider the possibility of pregnancy when prescribing this drug to women of reproductive age, particularly those who are sexually active, Grzeskowiak suggested. That does not mean doctors should avoid prescribing the antibiotic to these women, he emphasized; rather, clinicians should consider pregnancy prepares and medical history when choosing a treatment.

In some cases, doxycycline may still be the best option for a severe infection, Winterstein told Live Science, and that infection could itself put a pregnancy at risk. But for less-serious infections, safer alternatives may be available, she noted.

#141. Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1449 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising latest concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies.
  • Industry observers note that the findings were particularly concerning among younger adults.
  • Sources indicate that researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising latest concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients.

Industry observers note that the findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.

Sources indicate that researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination.

Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health.

Recent findings suggest that the energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants.

Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease.

A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee).

However, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee.

In a recent development, another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market.

In a recent development, "These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products.".

FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events.

Sources indicate that to investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients.

In a recent development, the comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025.

Several differences stood out in the analysis:.

These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack.

In a recent development, "Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula stated.

Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable.

One of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group.

In a recent development, several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies.

In a recent development, how the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications.

These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults.

Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks?

Although the results raise key questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause.

It has been revealed that "This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," stated Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.".

It has been revealed that marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health.

In a recent development, because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role.

How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports.

The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025.

Sources indicate that of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group.

Researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine).

Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another.

The researchers also highlighted key limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction.

In a recent development, just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report.

Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements.

Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them.

#140. A robot has assembled a structure in space for the first time

A robot has assembled a structure in space for the first time

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Source: Newscientist

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Check your subscription status, update your details and more.
  • A robot has built a structure in space without any help of astronauts.
  • It has been revealed that sergio Pellegrino at the California Institute of Technology and his team developed their robot as part of a US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) initiative to explore new ways to build in space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check your subscription status, update your details and more.

A robot has built a structure in space without any help of astronauts. The first-of-its-kind achievement is a step towards autonomous in-orbit manufacturing and assembly of structures such as space stations and data centres, which will be crucial if we want to develop an orbital economy.

It has been revealed that sergio Pellegrino at the California Institute of Technology and his team developed their robot as part of a US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) initiative to explore new ways to build in space. Large orbiting structures in the past have either been assembled with the help of astronauts or launched pre-assembled and folded up, spring-loaded to unfold upon release from their capsules.

But unfolding doesn’t work for more complex structures, and sending astronauts to build space stations isn’t cost-effective. “We’ve been unfolding things in space, there’s been a lot of unfolding,” states Pellegrino. “The big picture is how are we going to transition from unfolding in space to building in space.”.

Putting data centres in space isn’t going to happen any time soon.

The robot that he and his team built is essentially a sophisticated arm that picks up parts and clicks them together in a process similar to putting up a tent or playing with a toy construction set. The precision involved in the movements makes this more difficult than one might expect, especially because the researchers only had 18 months to take the whole project from idea to execution in orbit.

Sources indicate that since its March launch from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California, the robot has been working on building a radio antenna, 1.4 metres in diameter, from a set of tubes, joints and reflective nets. As it went along, images of each step were beamed back to Earth, where the researchers checked them and troubleshot any problems with an identical robot in their lab. Construction of the antenna hasn’t quite been completed and the mission ends in December, but work has proceeded far enough to prove that this is a viable approach, states Pellegrino.

Sources indicate that now that it has had its first test, Pellegrino hopes that other researchers and space-flight businesses get onboard to accelerate development of faster, larger assembly systems. “I think our objective should be that in the next 5 years we start doing some of this, and in 10 years, there is the beginning for a real maturing infrastructure,” he indicates.

Eventually, the goal is to build much larger structures, with less troubleshooting from the ground.

Taking space-based construction out of human hands could accelerate the development of businesses and science in orbit enormously, and putting together one radio antenna in space is just the beginning.

#139. Scientists Discover Upcoming Form of Prostate Cancer

Scientists Discover Upcoming Form of Prostate Cancer

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of British Columbia have identified a previously unrecognized form of hereditary prostate cancer linked to a rare genetic mutation that can lead to aggressive disease at relatively young ages.
  • The fresh study, published in Cancer Discovery, connects this form of hereditary prostate cancer to inherited mutations in a gene called CDK12.
  • Scientists previously believed that harmful CDK12 mutations developed spontaneously within tumor cells rather than being inherited from a parent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of British Columbia have identified a previously unrecognized form of hereditary prostate cancer linked to a rare genetic mutation that can lead to aggressive disease at relatively young ages. The discovery could help doctors identify families with an inherited cancer risk and introduce earlier screening, potentially detecting tumors before they spread.

The fresh study, published in Cancer Discovery, connects this form of hereditary prostate cancer to inherited mutations in a gene called CDK12. After analyzing genetic data from more than 4,500 people with aggressive prostate cancer, researchers identified five unrelated men carrying these mutations. All five developed metastatic prostate cancer between ages 44 and 62.

Scientists previously believed that harmful CDK12 mutations developed spontaneously within tumor cells rather than being inherited from a parent. To investigate whether inherited mutations were responsible for the cancers, researchers examined the patients’ tumors for a distinctive pattern of genetic changes associated with CDK12 dysfunction.

In a recent development, “The tumors provided us with a genetic signature that pointed directly back to CDK12,” said lead author Dr. Sofie Tolmeijer, a postdoctoral fellow in the Wyatt lab. “It gave us compelling evidence that these inherited mutations were playing a direct role in causing their cancer.”.

Industry observers note that “What’s striking is that every patient we identified with this inherited mutation had already developed metastatic disease by the time they were diagnosed,” noted senior author Dr. Alexander Wyatt, associate professor of urologic sciences at UBC and UBC President’s Excellence Chair in Precision Oncology. “The opportunity now is to identify these families earlier and give people the chance to benefit from enhanced screening, when there are still curative treatment options.”.

Sources indicate that approximately 5 to 10 percent of cancers are associated with inherited genetic mutations, rather than changes that accumulate during a person’s lifetime. Among the best-known examples are BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations, which increase the risk of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and prostate cancers. Genetic testing for these mutations already helps guide cancer screening and preventive care.

It has been revealed that inherited CDK12 mutations appear considerably rarer. The researchers estimate that they occur in approximately one in 1,000 people with aggressive prostate cancer, potentially affecting hundreds of families worldwide. Identifying a carrier could allow relatives to undergo genetic testing and determine whether they share the mutation.

Industry observers note that “While this mutation is extremely rare, the discovery could be lifesaving for the families who carry it,” stated Dr. Tolmeijer. “Finding one person with an inherited mutation gives us the opportunity to identify other family members at risk and help them take action before cancer develops or spreads.”.

The research team recommends considering CDK12 for inclusion in standard hereditary prostate cancer testing panels. Unlike genetic discoveries that require new diagnostic methods, CDK12 mutations can already be detected using existing clinical technology, potentially making expanded testing faster and less expensive to implement.

“One of the most exciting aspects of this discovery is that we already have the technology needed to act on it,” noted Dr. Wyatt, who is also a senior research scientist at the Vancouver Prostate Centre and senior scientist at BC Cancer. “Adding CDK12 to existing genetic tests is relatively straightforward, which means this discovery could move from the research lab into clinical care much more promptly.”.

The findings also raise questions about whether inherited CDK12 mutations contribute to ovarian cancer. Several affected men had family histories of ovarian cancer, and researchers identified an additional person with ovarian cancer who carried an inherited CDK12 mutation. That person’s tumor displayed the same characteristic genetic changes associated with CDK12 dysfunction. Further research is needed to establish whether the mutation increases ovarian cancer risk.

“With the right genetic testing and screening programs, we envision a future where no one who inherits one of these mutations dies from cancer,” said Dr. Wyatt.

You should turn them off when sleeping or left unattended. Common overnight hazards like a unit tipping over, bedding sitting too close to the heater, or an outlet overheating pose significant risks that you might not notice until you wake up. While most space heaters have preventative safety features like automatic shutoff or built-in thermostats, and may even be rated for continuous use, it’s best to resist the temptation of 24-hour warmth for safer operation.

#137. Tech Report: Chinese graduate students are now choosing to stay closer to home

Tech Report: Chinese graduate students are now choosing to stay closer to home

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Nature

💡 Key Takeaways
  • You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS.
  • Hong Kong is expected to have around 35,000 more students from the Chinese mainland enrolled in its higher-education institutions in 2030 than in 2025.
  • Analysis of global higher-education trends indicates that Chinese students are increasingly choosing to stay in Asia to further their studies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hong Kong is expected to have around 35,000 more students from the Chinese mainland enrolled in its higher-education institutions in 2030 than in 2025. Credit: Vernon Yuen/NurPhoto via Getty.

Analysis of global higher-education trends indicates that Chinese students are increasingly choosing to stay in Asia to further their studies.

Recent findings suggest that zhao Junyi is one of many postgraduate students who are rerouting back to Asia after studying elsewhere. Originally from Beijing, Zhao started a four-year PhD programme in planetary science at the University of Hong Kong in September. He’s happy about his choice.

In Hong Kong, Zhao notes, he can stay abreast of updates from China’s space programme in an English-speaking, international environment, as well as “connect with the research community and collaborate with colleagues from Europe and the United States”.

Hong Kong is a special administrative region of China and has a different education system from the Chinese mainland. Therefore, students from the Chinese mainland studying in Hong Kong are thought of as studying ‘overseas’.

Zhao obtained his bachelor’s degree in astronomy earlier this year from the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. He claims he decided against furthering his studies in the United States partly because of the federal government’s cuts to scientific funding. He didn’t go back to the Chinese mainland because only those with a master’s degree can apply for doctoral courses there, whereas Hong Kong doesn’t have such a requirement, he explains.

Industry observers note that china’s rapid advancements in space exploration are also a massive draw. Zhao’s current supervisor is analysing lunar samples collected by China’s Chang’e-5 and Chang’e-6 space missions. For Zhao, who grew up as a fan of the Chang’e programme, it is a dream come true to learn about its progress first-hand and to potentially be a part of it himself.

“Hong Kong is so attractive in so many ways,” claims Zhao, who is on a university scholarship that covers his tuition fees, rent and life expenses.

Zhao is among a growing crop of Chinese students who are seeking degrees in Asia rather than in the West.

The shift can be felt most strongly in Malaysia, Hong Kong and Macau. These are the places projected to have the fastest increase in the number of enrolled students from the Chinese mainland between 2025 and 2030, according to figures shared with Nature by London-based consultancy Quacquarelli Symonds (QS), which analyses global higher-education institutions and student mobility (see ‘Student flows’).

For the wealthy, English-speaking countries that have been popular with Chinese students for decades, the projections by QS point in the opposite direction. The United States, Australia and Canada will see the number of Chinese enrolments decrease year-on-year, with the United Kingdom holding steady. The drop in the number of students headed for the United States is projected to happen particularly quickly.

The trend demonstrates that prospective Chinese students now consider a wider combination of factors, including how far the host country is from home and how easily they can find a job with their degree, notes Alice Wei, a consultant at QS.

Industry observers note that for Zhao, one of the most exciting things about studying in Hong Kong is that it means he can visit home easily, especially for vital occasions. “I couldn’t go home for the Chinese Latest Year for many years when I was in the United States because it was not a public holiday there.”.

The number of Chinese students studying in US universities is projected to fall by an average of 4% each year between 2025 and 2030, the sharpest drop of all countries and territories assessed.

Industry observers note that students from China — and other countries — are facing more restrictions during and after their time in the United States, Wei says. For example, the US federal government in July proposed putting a hard limit on the duration of visas issued to foreign students and requires them to pack up and leave within 30 days of their programmes ending. Another US proposal suggests a US$100,000 fee for international students if they intend to stay to work after graduating. Australia and Canada have also introduced tougher immigration rules for foreign students.

According to recent reports, australia is projected to overtake the United States as the leading study destination for Chinese students by 2030.Credit: Dr. Victor Wong / Shutterstock.

Industry observers note that geopolitical tensions are another deterrent. US-based researchers are increasingly being scrutinized over their collaboration with Chinese partners as the United States enhances research security. For Zhao and other prospective students from China, such efforts make it harder for them to imagine a future in the United States.

“Because I am a Chinese national, it would be nearly impossible for me to participate in NASA’s research programmes,” Zhao says. NASA has blocked Chinese citizens from joining its programme out of security concerns.

Simultaneously, various factors are pulling Chinese students closer to home.

In a recent development, shorter geographical distances and familiar lifestyles are two possible selling points. Malaysia, for example, is projected to see an annual rise of 13% in the number of Chinese enrolments between 2025 and 2030, the highest growth in QS’s analysis.

Malaysia’s sizeable community of people who speak Mandarin or Chinese dialects makes Chinese students feel at home in the southeast Asian country, says Ngeow Chow Bing, director of the Institute of China Studies at the University of Malaya in Kuala Lumpur. A visa-free travel policy between the two nations also means that their relatives can visit them whenever they want, he says.

Sources indicate that it is hard to compare Chinese students in Malaysia directly with those in the West, because they study different disciplines, Ngeow claims. For example, Chinese students going to the United States are more likely to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics, but in Malaysia, the “vast majority” study social sciences and languages, he says. “Malaysia is still not yet very renowned for science and tech,” he notes.

Sources indicate that in South Korea, the fourth fastest-growing destination on the list — with a yearly increase in enrolment rates of 8% — it is the country’s high-tech manufacturing industries that attract Chinese students, such as those for semiconductor chips, biopharmaceutical and advanced materials, says Xie Yuzhen, a Shanghai-based independent researcher who studies China’s higher-education industry. Students can gain first-hand experience in these industries owing to the close relationship between significant companies and universities, Xie says.

Junsuk Rho, a materials scientist at Pohang University of Science and Technology in South Korea, has observed an influx of Chinese graduate students to the country over the past few years.

#136. Blood Vessel Function Improved Just 60 Minutes After Taking This Anti-Aging Supplement

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (857 words)
General 🌐 Scitechdaily

Blood Vessel Function Improved Just 60 Minutes After Taking This Anti-Aging Supplement

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blood vessel function improved within an hour of a supplement’s first dose in a small human trial, though lasting protection against cardiovascular disease remains unproven.
  • What if protecting the heart and blood vessels requires more than treating traditional risk factors such as high blood pressure and cholesterol?
  • Cardiovascular disease remains the world’s leading cause of death, and researchers at the University of Surrey are exploring whether targeting the biology of aging could help protect the heart and blood vessels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blood vessel function improved within an hour of a supplement’s first dose in a small human trial, though lasting protection against cardiovascular disease remains unproven.

What if protecting the heart and blood vessels requires more than treating traditional risk factors such as high blood pressure and cholesterol?

Cardiovascular disease remains the world’s leading cause of death, and researchers at the University of Surrey are exploring whether targeting the biology of aging could help protect the heart and blood vessels. In a small trial, they tested a nutritional supplement designed to address several aging-related processes at once, finding improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure over six months.

It has been revealed that the randomized controlled trial enrolled 61 participants, with 33 taking NOVOS Core and 28 receiving a placebo once daily for six months. Researchers investigated whether combining these substances could improve cardiovascular health by influencing multiple aging-related pathways simultaneously.

Recent findings suggest that the supplement combines 12 ingredients selected to target biological processes associated with aging. These include glycine, magnesium malate, calcium alpha-ketoglutarate, glucosamine sulfate, vitamin C, L-theanine, hyaluronic acid, and small amounts of lithium, along with plant-derived compounds such as fisetin, pterostilbene, Rhodiola rosea extract, and ginger extract.

Professor Christian Heiss, Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Surrey, remarked: “Biological aging is not driven by one pathway, but by a number of interacting molecular and cellular processes. The idea behind this study was to ask whether addressing several of these processes at the same time via a nutritional supplement could produce measurable effects on cardiovascular health biomarkers.

Sources indicate that “As a first step, we looked at established biomarkers of vascular health, such as blood pressure and cholesterol levels, rather than clinical outcomes. We found favorable changes in endothelial function, arterial stiffness, and systolic blood pressure after six months. These findings are encouraging. We now need larger studies to understand the mechanisms involved and, importantly, whether these changes translate into longer-term health benefits.”.

Researchers measured flow-mediated dilation, or how readily an artery widens as blood flow increases. This reveals how well its inner lining, the endothelium, works to regulate vessel width and blood clotting. Dilation improved in the supplement group compared with the placebo group after six months. An improvement also appeared just one hour after the first dose, while placebo readings remained largely unchanged.

Recent findings suggest that arteries were also less stiff in the supplement group. Researchers assessed this using pulse wave velocity, the speed at which a pressure wave travels through arteries. Slower waves indicate more flexible arteries, and the adjusted difference between groups was 1.18 meters per second after six months.

Systolic blood pressure, the pressure when the heart contracts, was an adjusted 6.1 mmHg lower in the supplement group than in the placebo group at six months. A difference was also observed one hour after the first dose. Estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk decreased modestly, largely reflecting the blood pressure difference.

Recent findings suggest that previous large studies have associated a sustained 5 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure with approximately 10 percent fewer major cardiovascular events. The Surrey trial measured markers associated with risk and was not designed to determine whether participants experienced fewer such events.

Diogo Barardo, PhD, Director of R&D at NOVOS and a geroscientist, a scientist specializing in the biology of aging, stated:.

“When we began developing NOVOS Core in 2019, our hypothesis was that simultaneously targeting all the hallmarks of aging, the fundamental biological processes underlying aging and age-related diseases, could produce measurable improvements in the organs and systems affected by aging.

“The STAMINA results provide encouraging clinical evidence consistent with that hypothesis, demonstrating improvements across three measures of cardiovascular function, particularly meaningful given that cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide.”.

Blood tests showed no significant changes in cholesterol or other blood lipids, suggesting that lipid lowering did not explain the improvements in blood vessel measures.

Professor Juliet Wright, Founding Dean of the School of Medicine at the University of Surrey, said:.

“This study is a good example of how ideas emerging from the biology of aging can be tested rigorously in people. The findings provide an interesting proof of concept, but the important next step is to understand the underlying biology and establish whether changes in cardiovascular biomarkers translate into meaningful longer-term health benefits.”.

Reference: “Acute and 6-month vascular effects of a multi-component nutritional supplement: a randomized controlled trial” by Charles Piercy, Jenny Harris, Kenza Sackho, Paola Campagnolo, Diogo Barardo, Ben Creagh-Brown and Christian Heiss, 4 November 2026, European Heart Journal Open. DOI: 10.1093/ehjopen/oeag157.

Sources indicate that the investigator-initiated study was supported by NOVOS Labs through provision of the study supplement known as NOVOS Core and matching control and an unrestricted contribution towards research costs. NOVOS Labs had no role in study design, collection, or primary interpretation of the data, or the decision to publish.

#135. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

📅 06 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words)
General 🌐 Sciencenews

This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every print subscription comes with full digital access.
  • The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater.
  • A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access.

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater.

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

According to recent reports, scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

It has been revealed that G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, indicates Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

According to recent reports, motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani indicates. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

Industry observers note that it wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

Industry observers note that for amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of Fresh South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these challenges. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

Industry observers note that G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

#133. Latest Update: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Latest Update: NASA reveals Earth's ozone hole has grown to a size not seen in a decade

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, reaching one of its largest sizes on record.
  • The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area.
  • Recent findings suggest that between September 7 and October 13, 2026, when ozone depletion was at its seasonal peak, the hole covered an average of approximately 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, reaching one of its largest sizes on record. Despite the striking increase, scientists from NASA and NOAA say Earth's protective ozone layer is continuing its gradual recovery and remains on track to heal later this century.

The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area. Scientists attributed the expansion primarily to an exceptionally strong polar vortex, a large circulation of winds that influences atmospheric conditions over Antarctica. They also emphasized that international efforts to reduce harmful chemicals have prevented the hole from becoming even larger.

Recent findings suggest that between September 7 and October 13, 2026, when ozone depletion was at its seasonal peak, the hole covered an average of approximately 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers). That is more than twice the size of the United States. Scientists closely monitor ozone in the stratosphere because it serves as Earth's natural "sunscreen," protecting living organisms from dangerous solar radiation. Unlike this beneficial layer high in the atmosphere, ozone near Earth's surface is a pollutant frequently associated with human activities.

Antarctica's Ozone Hole Reaches Its Largest Size in a Decade.

The ozone hole reached its maximum extent on September 18, spreading across 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). This was approximately 90% of the size of the largest ozone hole ever measured, which occurred on September 9, 2000.

"The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing," said Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland and longtime leader of NASA's ozone research team at the agency's Goddard Space Flight Center. "But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven't seen in a decade.".

Although the hole expanded to an extraordinary size, the results also demonstrate the benefits of decades of international environmental protections. Without reductions in chemicals known to destroy ozone, the affected area could have been substantially greater.

"The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak," Newman noted.

How a Powerful Polar Vortex Accelerates Ozone Loss.

Industry observers note that ozone depletion begins with chemicals released through human activities, particularly compounds containing chlorine and bromine. Atmospheric circulation transports these substances into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet radiation breaks them apart. The released chlorine and bromine atoms then participate in chemical reactions involving particles in Antarctic stratospheric clouds, leading to the destruction of ozone.

A major factor in this process is the stratospheric polar vortex, a seasonal band of strong winds that circles Antarctica. This circulation traps extremely cold air over the region, allowing the formation of the special clouds that help trigger ozone destruction. When the vortex becomes unusually strong or expansive, conditions favorable for ozone loss can persist across a larger area.

It has been revealed that in 2026, atmospheric disturbances that would normally weaken the vortex were unusually subdued. This allowed the circulation to remain powerful and helped create a broader region where ozone could be destroyed.

"The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September," said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. "That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the South Pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur.".

NASA and NOAA Measure the 2026 Ozone Hole.

Despite its exceptional geographic size, the 2026 ozone hole did not experience the same extreme levels of ozone loss observed during record-breaking events 10 or 20 years earlier.

According to recent reports, to measure ozone concentrations, NOAA researchers launched instruments attached to weather balloons from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory. They also collected readings using the Dobson Ozone Spectrophotometer, an optical device designed to measure atmospheric ozone. Their observations demonstrated that ozone levels directly above the South Pole fell to their lowest reading of 2026 on October 17, reaching 105 Dobson units.

Recent findings suggest that the Dobson unit is the standard measurement used to describe the total amount of ozone above a particular location. To illustrate the scale, 100 Dobson units would produce a layer of ozone just 1 millimeter thick, approximately the thickness of a dime, if all the ozone in the atmospheric column were compressed to standard temperature and pressure at sea level. The lowest ozone concentration ever measured over the South Pole was 92 Dobson units in October 2006.

Satellites provide another essential source of information. Since 1979, spaceborne instruments have helped scientists observe changes in the ozone layer and track its condition over time. The 2026 measurements included data from NASA's Aura satellite, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, a joint NASA and NOAA mission.

Why Earth's Ozone Layer Is Still Recovering.

Scientists say the latest observations reinforce evidence that international restrictions on ozone-destroying chemicals are working. Much of that progress can be traced to the Montreal Protocol, a global agreement adopted in 1987 to phase out substances responsible for damaging the ozone layer.

Under the agreement, countries committed to replacing harmful compounds such as chlorofluorocarbons with alternatives that pose less danger to atmospheric ozone. According to Stephen Montzka, a senior scientist at NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory, chlorine concentrations in the Antarctic stratosphere associated with ozone-depleting chemicals have declined by approximately one-third compared with their peak levels in the 1980s.

Recent findings suggest that these reductions are significant because chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting compounds were once common in refrigerators, air conditioning systems, building insulation, and other everyday products. Although many of these substances have been phased out, they can remain in the atmosphere for decades. Additional emissions can also occur when older equipment, materials, and landfill waste release chemicals that were manufactured years ago.

According to recent reports, because these compounds break down so slowly, repairing the ozone layer takes many decades. Nevertheless, continued monitoring by NASA and NOAA indicates that the long-term recovery is progressing. Even with unusually large seasonal ozone holes such as the one observed in 2026, scientists expect the Antarctic ozone hole to recover by the 2070s.

It has been revealed that the latest findings illustrate how exceptional atmospheric conditions can temporarily produce severe ozone depletion without reversing decades of environmental progress. They also highlight the lasting impact of international cooperation in protecting Earth's atmosphere.

Sources indicate that every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand.

Sources indicate that I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again.

Recent findings suggest that this is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky.

In a recent development, the Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up.

It has been revealed that but every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. How many Pleiades I can see can change depending on what I do during the next 10 minutes.

According to recent reports, the Pleiades, also known as Messier 45 (M45) or the "Seven Sisters," are an open star cluster in Taurus. They're one of the closest clusters to the solar system and some of the youngest stars you can see with the naked eye — just 100 million years old. They're basically newborns.

Sources indicate that in mid-November, they rise in the east in the early evening and climb higher as the night progresses, making this an excellent time to get acquainted with them. Look east after dark for a tiny, compact group of stars. If you know Orion, which rises later, the Pleiades are above and to the right of it from mid-northern latitudes. Nearby you'll also find orange Aldebaran and the much broader V-shaped Hyades cluster. The Hyades are closer to the sun, but their stars are about 625 million years old.

The name "Seven Sisters" creates an immediate observational trap: people assume they're supposed to see seven stars. That's not necessarily true. In fact, six is a common naked-eye result under decently dark conditions (note that the shape of the six brightest is like a mini Big Dipper/Plough), while people with sharp eyesight under darker skies may see more. The cluster itself contains about 1,000 stars. The number you personally distinguish depends on eyesight, sky brightness, atmospheric conditions and how well your eyes have adapted to darkness.

That makes M45 much more interesting to me than a simple tick-box target. So tonight, don't just find the Pleiades — count them.

I'm going to run my Pleiades eye test in stages. First, I'll step outside and look almost immediately. I'll count the individual stars I can distinguish without spending ages convincing myself about marginal ones. Then I'll wait. After about 10 minutes (without looking at my phone or bright outdoor lights, of course), I'll count again. Full dark adaptation takes considerably longer, but even 10 minutes can make an obvious difference when you've just come from a brightly lit house.

I'll then try my trusty 10x50 binoculars. This is where the experiment stops being subtle. The little naked-eye knot of brightness suddenly becomes a field filled with stars. The Pleiades don't just become brighter through binoculars. Their whole character changes because stars that were below my naked-eye threshold appear. I'll also use the averted vision technique, looking slightly to one side rather than directly at M45. It's one of the best demonstrations of the technique, with its fainter stars seemingly popping into view as your more light-sensitive peripheral vision takes over.

According to recent reports, the moon is returning to the evening sky this week, waxing from a thin crescent toward first quarter. It reaches first quarter around Nov. 17, so moonlight becomes progressively more noticeable during the first half of the night. Look southwest during twilight, and you'll see the beautiful sight of a crescent moon sporting Earthshine, sunlight reflected from Earth onto the moon's night side.

It has been revealed that overnight, Nov. 15-16, don't miss Mars and Jupiter in conjunction. The two planets will appear just over a degree apart, rising in the east during the evening before climbing high into the southern sky in the hours before sunrise.

Industry observers note that the following night, Nov. 17-18, the Leonid meteor shower peaks. This is one shower where staying up later actually matters. Leo, the constellation containing the shower's radiant, doesn't rise until late, so the better opportunity comes after midnight and toward the predawn hours.

According to recent reports, auriga, "the Charioteer," is easy to see in the northeastern and eastern sky during November evenings, but have you spied the asterism close to its brightest star, Capella? It's known as the "Goat Star," though its Latin name is the diminutive of capra, meaning "little she-goat." The reason is esoteric — Capella represents Amalthea, the mythological goat that suckled the infant Zeus — but there is a neat asterism (shape of stars) nearby that suddenly makes sense. Close to Capella is a triangle of faint stars that are known as The Kids — Epsilon, Zeta and Eta Aurigae — traditionally imagined as the offspring of Capella. It's one of those little patterns that makes a constellation much easier to recognize.

#131. Tech Report: You Were More Conscious as a Child Than You Are Now, Neuroscientist Claims

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1601 words)

Tech Report: You Were More Conscious as a Child Than You Are Now, Neuroscientist Claims

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • What if growing up makes you more knowledgeable but less aware of reality?
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if growing up makes you more knowledgeable but less aware of reality?

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

When you were a child, did you ever wonder what happened to the sea at the horizon? Perhaps you imagined it stretching forever. Or perhaps, like me, you believed that where the blue ended, the water simply fell off the edge of the world, spilling over in some enormous, invisible waterfall. It made perfect sense at the time, and there was quite a lot of magic involved, too. Then came geography lessons, maps, explanations, terminology, and the gradual realization that the world did not end where your vision did—that it was, in fact, far vaster than anything the eye could take in. So why has it become so difficult to recapture the purity and intensity of that experience as an adult?

Could there be a chance, however counterintuitive it sounds, that you were actually more conscious back then?

Recent findings suggest that it sounds counterintuitive, but Alysson Muotri, PhD, a professor of pediatrics and cellular and molecular medicine at the University of California, San Diego, has given this poetic—almost philosophical—idea scientific legs. To do so, he used one of the most futuristic tools that presently exists for investigating the human brain: brain organoids, tiny clusters of living neural tissue grown from stem cells in a laboratory. He wondered whether these tiny lumps of living human brain tissue could illuminate that elusive inner experience. What he found was that as we grow and learn about the world, this process might really be changing how we perceive reality.

But before you can explore consciousness in a lab, you need to build the organoids. The process begins with ordinary human cells, often collected from the skin. Scientists reprogram them into induced pluripotent stem cells, which regain the ability to develop into almost any cell type in the body. Researchers use chemical signals to turn these cells into neurons and other brain cells. The cells multiply, gathering into tiny clumps of tissue. Inside them, neurons begin making contact, and electrical signals pass between them. However, calling these organoids “brains in a dish” is rather generous, though tempting; they lack much of the anatomy of a developed human brain. Still, organoids allow scientists to watch human neural tissue take shape in ways that would be impossible to witness inside a living person’s skull.

Muotri’s team discovered in 2019 that maturing organoids produced electrical rhythms resembling certain features of brain activity recorded in premature infants. Here was human neural tissue, deprived of the sights and sounds accompanying a child’s development, nevertheless organizing itself into patterns observed in living brains. Four years later, researchers at Indiana University Bloomington incorporated brain organoids into an experimental computing system that used their electrical responses to help recognize spoken sounds and predict mathematical patterns. By 2025, other scientists had reported that repeated electrical stimulation could alter how individual neurons in organoids responded, with some changes lingering for hours after the stimulation came to a halt—evidence of cellular mechanisms associated with learning and memory.

Muotri, meanwhile, had begun wondering whether the electrical activity of his brain organoids could offer any clues to that elusive inner experience we call consciousness. Of course, even if we assume that consciousness arises entirely from the brain, there is something peculiar about trying to measure it. It’s not as though you can insert a thermometer into someone’s head and pinpoint the experience of being alive and aware—or the feeling of experiencing the world as a child.

Sources indicate that muotri decided to investigate by borrowing an approach from consciousness research called the perturbational complexity index (PCI). In humans, the method involves delivering a brief magnetic pulse to the brain and recording the resulting electrical activity through electrodes placed on the scalp. Earlier researchers have analyzed the responses and calculated a score that has helped distinguish wakefulness from deep sleep and general anesthesia; a higher score indicates greater conscious awareness. While PCI cannot measure consciousness directly, it offers clues about the brain’s capacity to sustain it.

Industry observers note that in preliminary findings, Muotri measured the organoids’ electrical activity before exposing them to repeated stimulation, using an approach similar to PCI. To say that he found a startling degree of complexity in the way their neurons communicate with one another—with scores that exceeded those typically recorded in awake human brains—is an understatement. Because the organoid and human measurements use different methods, however, the scores cannot be compared directly. Still, he wasn’t expecting the organoids to have this PCI level, he notes. “It’s very latest, and I’m still thinking about what it means.”.

It has been revealed that muotri also found something shocking about how the organoids behaved as they were stimulated repeatedly with light. Gradually, the cells began reacting differently to the stimulation, and some of those changes lingered after the light was switched off. “So there is some kind of a memory embedded in those networks,” he says. But even more astounding was that, as the organoids adapted to the stimulation, their complexity score actually fell, similar to the way human brains with lower PCI scores were less aware.

In a recent development, he thinks the reason is that a brain organoid increases its bias as it learns, just as we become more biased as we learn more over the years. By bias, Muotri means that experience makes certain neural responses, particularly those reinforced through repeated exposure, more likely than others. Learning, apparently, does more than give us knowledge. It may also condition us to overlook parts of the world we once experienced more freely.

It has been revealed that “It’s almost like when you are born…as soon as your brain is naive and fresh, you’re more conscious than when you are an adult,” Muotri continues. By adulthood, however, experience has cramped your brain’s style. “Because you already experienced so many things, you’re already [so] attached to the physical environment, that you become less conscious than you were [as] a baby.”.

The suggestion is extraordinary, especially coming from experiments involving tissue that has never seen a sunset, heard a lullaby, obeyed a teacher, or encountered anything resembling a childhood whatsoever.

Sources indicate that yet there is a recognizable human parallel. Developmental psychologist Alison Gopnik has compared adult attention to a spotlight, concentrated on what matters for an immediate goal, and children’s attention to a lantern, illuminating more of their surroundings. A toddler entering an unfamiliar room might become absorbed by a patch of sunlight that an adult barely notices. The adult knows more about the room, but familiarity helps determine what deserves attention. Noticing more of the world doesn’t necessarily mean being more conscious of it.

Sources indicate that however, a baby’s brain, already shaped by months of development in the womb, is hardly comparable to an organoid that has never experienced the world outside a laboratory. That’s why Kenneth Kosik, MD, a neuroscience professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara, is skeptical. In a 2024 paper published in the journal Patterns, titled Why Brain Organoids Are Not Conscious Yet, he argued that organoids lack much of the organization and communication between brain regions that may be necessary for consciousness. And electrical activity, however complicated, is not enough to prove an inner life. Neurons firing independently can produce unpredictable signals that are difficult to reduce to a simpler description, even when there is no evidence that anything is being experienced. “So we still have a little bit of a jump there, yeah, to say that compressibility is related to consciousness,” Kosik notes.

Sources indicate that muotri himself is cautious about what the numbers mean and says they are still preliminary data. Nor does he claim that his organoids actually experience anything. “I should not say they are conscious outright,” he says.

According to recent reports, for now, Muotri’s experiments cannot definitively tell us whether we were more conscious as children than we are as adults, but they do open a window onto something just as intriguing: what happens to our experience of the world if learning itself changes how our brains encounter our environment? After all, the day I discovered that the sea did not plunge into an abyss, I gained precious knowledge that generations before me had strived to acquire. But have I ever again experienced the sea quite as fully as I did when I was a child, believing it could spill over the world’s edge? That is a whole different question, and we don’t have the answer yet.

Stav Dimitropoulos is a Gold and Community Anthem Award–winning journalist, and writes about consciousness, science, and culture for Popular Mechanics, Nature, and the BBC. Her work often explores mind-stretching angles where science meets philosophy. Her debut nonfiction book, Slow, Lazy, Gluttons (Greystone Books, 2026) asks: What if the traits society shames — laziness, darkness, nostalgia, and more — are actually survival superpowers?

#130. Scientists Warn of a Disturbing Rise in Vitamin K Deficiency Among American Newborns

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words)
General 🌐 Scitechdaily

Scientists Warn of a Disturbing Rise in Vitamin K Deficiency Among American Newborns

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Scitechdaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Only about one in five infants diagnosed with vitamin K-related bleeding had received the shot, U.S.
  • Sources indicate that babies are born with little vitamin K, leaving them vulnerable to bleeding that can cause permanent brain damage or death.
  • That trend has coincided with a sharp rise in diagnoses of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin-K-deficient bleeding (VKDB).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Only about one in five infants diagnosed with vitamin K-related bleeding had received the shot, U.S. health records show.

Sources indicate that babies are born with little vitamin K, leaving them vulnerable to bleeding that can cause permanent brain damage or death. A single shot helps protect against that danger. The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended one dose injected into a muscle for newborns since 1961, and a growing number of American parents are choosing to skip it.

That trend has coincided with a sharp rise in diagnoses of vitamin K deficiency (VKD) and vitamin-K-deficient bleeding (VKDB). A nationwide study found that their rates increased by 216% and 347%, respectively, between 2017 and 2025, while the percentage of newborns receiving injectable vitamin K fell from 97.7% to 95.0%. The findings were published on November 5, 2026, in JAMA Pediatrics.

Vitamin K activates specialized proteins needed for normal blood clotting. Newborns receive too little through the placenta, absorb it poorly through their digestive systems, and get little from breast milk. The injection addresses a deficiency at a time when its consequences can be severe.

Recent findings suggest that classical VKD occurs between 2 days and 1 week after birth and causes bruising and bleeding from the umbilicus, or belly button. Late VKD, which occurs between 1 week and 6 months of age, carries a 30% to 60% risk of intracranial hemorrhage, or bleeding inside the skull. That bleeding can lead to seizures, permanent brain damage, or death.

Refusal of the shot has increased over the past decade. Previous studies found that the proportion of newborns who did not receive intramuscular vitamin K rose from 2.9% in 2017 to 5.2% in 2024.

To investigate the consequences of that trend, Elizabeth Wolf, M.D., MPH, led the latest nationwide study. Wolf is a pediatrician at Children’s Hospital of Richmond at VCU and an associate professor in the Department of Pediatrics at Virginia Commonwealth University School of Medicine.

Sources indicate that the researchers analyzed de-identified electronic health records from a large national database covering health systems across the United States. Their analysis included more than 11 million infants aged 0 to 6 months who were born at 35 weeks’ gestation or later and received care between 2017 and 2025.

Only 40% of infants diagnosed with VKD and about 19% of those diagnosed with VKDB had received vitamin K shots. About 7% of infants with VKD and 2% of those with VKDB also had a diagnosis of intracranial or intracerebral hemorrhage, meaning bleeding inside the skull or within the brain tissue itself.

“We knew from prior studies that vitamin K refusal had been increasing in the U.S., and we wanted to learn if there were any real-life consequences of this trend,” Wolf mentioned. “We found that the answer is undeniably yes, with the rates of VKD and VKDB multiplying over the course of our study.”.

The researchers caution that the simultaneous decline in injections and increase in diagnoses does not prove causation. Wolf considers other explanations unlikely, however, because behaviors and diseases that increase the risk of VKD remained constant or decreased during the study period.

Recent findings suggest that the study’s co-authors included Steven Woolf, M.D., director emeritus of the VCU Center on Society and Health and a professor in VCU School of Medicine’s Department of Family Medicine, Evan French, MS, of VCU’s C. Kenneth and Dianne Wright Center for Clinical and Translational Research, and Darya Shokouhi Niaki, Pharm.D., of the VCU School of Public Health’s Department of Biostatistics.

Wolf connected the findings to growing mistrust of doctors and public health professionals.

Sources indicate that “Similar to the recent measles outbreaks, we are seeing the real-world implications of growing mistrust of doctors and public health professionals. We need clear messaging from all levels of public health about the benefits of vitamin K administration for newborns.”.

According to recent reports, like childhood vaccines, the researchers say, vitamin K has been “a victim of its own success,” with many parents unaware that refusing the shot can have serious lifelong consequences. Wolf says more research is needed to determine how best to communicate the seriousness of vitamin K deficiency and encourage use of the medication in newborns.

“We should continue to follow these trends moving forward since the rates of vitamin K deficiency and vitamin-K-deficient bleeding may continue to rise if vitamin K refusal keeps increasing. We need to better understand why parents are refusing vitamin K and what can be done to improve the uptake of this key medication,” Wolf stated.

Reference: “Vitamin K Deficiency and Associated Bleeding in Infants” by Elizabeth R. Wolf, Evan French, Darya Shokouhi Niaki and Steven H. Woolf, 5 November 2026, JAMA Pediatrics. DOI: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.5794.
