#99. Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1635 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Colorectal cancer is rising again after 20 years, and scientists don't know why

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults.
  • Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50.
  • Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that colorectal cancer rates are climbing again in the United States after more than two decades of decline, and the troubling increase is affecting far more than younger adults. Upcoming research published in NEJM Evidence reveals that the disease is becoming more common across nearly every age group under 70, raising concerns about a growing public health challenge.

Colorectal cancer is already the second leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States and the leading cause among adults younger than 50. Although rising cases in younger people have attracted widespread attention, the latest findings show that the problem extends into older generations. Researchers warn that a continued increase could place additional pressure on the healthcare system as more patients require cancer treatment and long-term care after diagnosis.

Colorectal Cancer Rates Reverse Decades of Decline.

In a recent development, to investigate the changing pattern, Caitlin Murphy, PhD, MPH, Professor of Pediatrics and Public Health Sciences at the University of Chicago, and her colleagues examined the latest colorectal cancer incidence data from the National Cancer Institute. Their analysis tracked changes in diagnoses from 2000 through 2023.

The results revealed a significant reversal. In 2000, the age-adjusted colorectal cancer incidence rate was 55.2 cases per 100,000 people. By 2022, that figure had dropped to 36.7. However, the rate increased to 38.3 in 2023, marking the first overall rise after more than two decades of falling rates.

Industry observers note that "This is the first time that we have seen an increase in the overall rate since in more than 20 years," Murphy remarked. She emphasized that the long-standing downward trend had been a major feature of colorectal cancer statistics for decades. The new analysis indicates that rates are now increasing in every age group through ages 65 to 69.

In a recent development, murphy, an epidemiologist who specializes in colorectal cancer patterns, had anticipated that the increase initially observed in younger adults would eventually become apparent among older people. She attributes this expected progression to a phenomenon called the "birth cohort effect.".

According to recent reports, this effect describes how people born during the same general period can share risk patterns that become more apparent as they grow older. In this case, individuals born in the 1960s and subsequent decades appear to face an elevated risk of colorectal cancer as they enter middle age and later life.

It has been revealed that "I think of a birth cohort effect as the interaction of age and time," Murphy explained. "As people born around the same time move through time and age together, we're going to see more colorectal cancers being diagnosed.".

A Sharp Increase Among Adults Ages 45 to 49.

One of the most striking findings involved people between 45 and 49 years old. From 2019 through 2023, colorectal cancer incidence in this group increased by 12.76% annually, the largest rise recorded among the age groups examined.

Researchers believe much of this particular increase can be explained by changes in cancer screening recommendations. National guidelines lowered the recommended starting age for routine colorectal cancer screening from 50 to 45, allowing more people to be tested and more previously undetected cancers to be identified.

"That means that screening is doing as we intend it to do -- it's catching cancer earlier," Murphy said.

But increased screening cannot account for the broader pattern. Colorectal cancer rates are also rising among adults ages 65 to 69, while the decline has stalled among those ages 70 to 74. Both populations have historically experienced substantial benefits from screening, and approximately 80% of people in these age groups are current with recommended testing.

These findings are particularly concerning because they suggest that additional, unidentified risk factors could be counteracting some of the progress achieved through decades of cancer screening.

According to recent reports, the research team also investigated whether disruptions during the COVID-19 pandemic might have distorted the results. Cancer screenings and diagnoses were affected during the pandemic, potentially changing when cases were detected. However, the upward trend remained even after the researchers removed data from 2020 and 2021. Screening activity had also largely recovered to its earlier levels by January 2021, making pandemic-related disruptions an unlikely explanation for the increase recorded in 2023.

"These results motivate us to understand reasons for this rise, so risk factors can be identified and possibly reduced," noted Sonia Kupfer, MD, director of the Gastrointestinal Cancer Risk and Prevention Clinic at UChicago Medicine.

Why Colorectal Cancer Is Rising Across Generations.

The growing number of colorectal cancer diagnoses among younger Americans has become a major health concern. American Cancer Society data show that incidence among adults ages 20 to 49 increased by approximately 3% per year between 2013 and 2022.

Sources indicate that this increase in colorectal cancer among people younger than 50, often referred to as early-onset colorectal cancer, has drawn considerable public and scientific attention. The latest study suggests that understanding why younger adults are developing the disease more frequently could also help explain what is happening in older populations.

"There are many unique challenges when you're diagnosed with cancer at a young age, so it's important that we shine a spotlight on that problem," Murphy remarked. "But in terms of understanding the root cause, I think our study indicates that we can consider that whatever might be causing colorectal cancer in younger people is now also causing it to increase in older people as well.".

The underlying causes remain uncertain, but researchers are investigating whether exposure to chemicals in the environment could play a role.

According to recent reports, murphy and her colleagues are working with Xin Hu, PhD, a toxicologist at Emory University, to examine this possibility. Their approach involves analyzing small blood samples for evidence of thousands of environmental chemical exposures simultaneously. By identifying which substances are associated with potential risks, the team hopes to narrow the list of chemicals that deserve more detailed investigation.

Industry observers note that the researchers then initiative to collaborate with Kupfer to explore how these chemicals affect colon tissue. To do so, they will use organoids, laboratory-grown models that reproduce crucial features of the colon. These miniature tissue systems allow scientists to study biological responses in a controlled environment and could help uncover how certain exposures contribute to colorectal cancer.

Why Colorectal Cancer Screening Remains Critical.

With cancer rates increasing across a broad range of ages, the researchers emphasize the need to keep tracking national cancer statistics as new registry information becomes available each year.

Sources indicate that murphy cautions that the consequences could become substantial if the current pattern continues. As large numbers of Americans born in more recent decades grow older, rising incidence rates could translate into many additional cancer diagnoses. That would increase demand for medical treatment and services supporting people who survive colorectal cancer.

While scientists work to understand the factors behind the increase, screening remains one of the most effective ways to find colorectal cancer early and reduce the risk of dying from the disease.

According to recent reports, current national recommendations advise adults at average risk to begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45 and continue through age 75. For people younger than 45 or older than 75, screening decisions should be tailored to individual circumstances, including family medical history, symptoms, and other health conditions.

Industry observers note that colonoscopy continues to be considered the gold standard for colorectal cancer screening, but patients also have additional testing options. These include newer blood-based screening tests and stool tests that can be completed at home.

"There are several ways to do screening that should be discussed with a clinician, so people know what the different screening tests are intended for and how often these need to be repeated," Kupfer added.

She also stressed that people younger than 45 should not ignore possible warning signs simply because they have not reached the age recommended for routine screening. Those without known genetic or family history risk factors should still seek medical attention if they notice blood in their stool, persistent changes in bowel habits, or unexplained weight loss.

The research, titled "Colorectal cancer among U.S. adults, 2000-2023," received financial support from the National Institutes of Health and the Eli and Edythe Broad Center of Regenerative Medicine and Stem Cell Research Ablon Scholars Program.

It has been revealed that along with Murphy, the study's authors include Folasade P. May of the University of California Los Angeles, Xin Hu of Emory University in Atlanta, and Samir Gupta of the University of California San Diego.

The University of Chicago's medical and biological sciences programs are also continuing to expand their work in cancer research and patient care. In April 2027, UChicago Medicine is scheduled to open the AbbVie Foundation Cancer Pavilion, which will be Chicago's first freestanding cancer pavilion. The facility is intended to bring together advanced diagnostic services, new cancer treatments, research that translates laboratory discoveries into clinical care, and comprehensive support for patients and the surrounding community.

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

Recent findings suggest that but the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”.

Recent findings suggest that for the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

Sources indicate that by year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”.

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

Industry observers note that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have tech giant this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

In a recent development, 2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is right now orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.

#94. Most of the deep ocean food supply in the Gulf of Mexico suddenly vanished, and most scientists blame the Deepwater Horizon oil spill

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words)
General 🌐 Earth

Most of the deep ocean food supply in the Gulf of Mexico suddenly vanished, and most scientists blame the Deepwater Horizon oil spill

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deep-sea fish, krill and squid in the Gulf of Mexico fell 60 to 85 percent after 2011, and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill is the leading suspect.
  • Marine biologists have always assumed the deep ocean is the safest and most stable ecosystem on the planet.
  • Unfortunately, a massive die-off in the Gulf of Mexico just proved that assumption is dangerously incorrect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deep-sea fish, krill and squid in the Gulf of Mexico fell 60 to 85 percent after 2011, and the Deepwater Horizon oil spill is the leading suspect.

Marine biologists have always assumed the deep ocean is the safest and most stable ecosystem on the planet. Because it is so vast and isolated from human life, they believed it was practically impossible to destroy.

Unfortunately, a massive die-off in the Gulf of Mexico just proved that assumption is dangerously incorrect.

In a recent development, between 2011 and 2015, the fish, shrimp, krill and squid living in the dark water below about 650 feet (200 meters) lost 60 to 85 percent of their numbers. Surveys through 2023 have not found them coming back.

It has been revealed that the crash indicates up in two records. One is the nets that scientists have towed through the same patch of ocean in the Gulf of Mexico for 13 years. The other is ship sonar, whose echoes come back weaker when fewer animals are swimming below.

Nothing in the water itself, not temperature, oxygen or food, changed in step with it. The one event that did line up in time was the Deepwater Horizon oil spill. The authors consider this the most likely explanation.

Tracey Sutton of Nova Southeastern University led the work, with colleagues at Florida International University, the University of South Florida and NOAA.

It has been revealed that the paper is careful about what it can show. The spill’s role is inferred from timing and from the absence of any natural driver, not from an experiment.

In a recent development, the record begins in January 2011, three months after the well was sealed. A nine-month campaign towed a net through a grid of 46 stations across the northern Gulf of Mexico. That first campaign is the baseline against which everything since has been measured.

The same net, with six separate bags that open and close on command, was towed again on nine shorter cruises between 2015 and 2023.

Each tow sampled from the surface down to 4,900 feet (1,500 meters) in five depth bands, at noon and again at midnight.

Towing twice a day matters, because most of these animals rise thousands of feet toward the surface every night to feed and sink again at dawn.

Only samples from the Gulf of Mexico’s own water mass were compared, since the Loop Current, which enters from the south, carries fewer animals and would have muddied the count.

Industry observers note that fish numbers per unit of water dropped 63.5 percent between 2011 and the later cruises. Shrimp and krill together dropped 62 percent, and small squid and their relatives dropped 59.7 percent.

Recent findings suggest that the groups that feed almost everything else fell hardest. Krill dropped 72.8 percent and lanternfish 62.9 percent. Bristlemouths, tiny fish that may be the most numerous vertebrates on Earth, dropped 69 percent.

Sources indicate that the sonar agreed. Sound bouncing back from the top 650 feet (200 meters) at night, when the migrators are up feeding, was 40 percent weaker after 2011.

A drop that size over three and a half years is bigger than any change recorded over 60 years in the California Current. That is the only other long-running count of deep-sea fish.

In an interview with Earth.com, Sutton stated the fall itself is not the part that surprised him most. “The slow recovery is the most surprising finding, with the realization that this downward shift may be irreversible,” he said.

In a recent development, and the dense swarms that predators depend on nearly disappeared. Across 134 full-column tows in the whole series, only one catch after the decline held more fish than the leanest catch of 2011.

A crowd that shrinks fast can lose genetic variety, so the team sequenced three common lanternfish species collected between 2011 and 2023, the longest such record for any deep-sea animal.

In a recent development, two of the three highlighted it. In one species, a standard measure of genetic variety fell about 11 percent between 2011 and 2016, then recovered partway by 2023. A second species followed the same path a few years later. The third showed no clear trend.

Recent findings suggest that the same tows kept adding to the list of what lives down there. Sutton told Earth.com that the deep interior holds more kinds of animals than any other part of the Gulf of Mexico, coral reefs included.

Recent findings suggest that his team has recorded almost 200 fish species there for the first time since the work began, he remarked. That is about one in every nine fish species now known from the Gulf.

“Our knowledge of what lives in the deep ocean is incredibly poor,” he mentioned, “even in the best-studied systems in the world, like the Gulf.”.

Sources indicate that the authors checked their own methods first. The same net, the same crew and the same analysis ran across every year, so a change in gear can’t explain the drop.

Water temperature in the twilight zone from 650 to 2,000 feet (200 to 600 meters) barely moved from year to year, and the deep Gulf stayed well supplied with oxygen. The plankton these animals eat didn’t thin out either; in 2013, mid-decline, it was above average.

So the authors turned to the spill. The Deepwater Horizon blowout on April 20, 2010 released up to 4.9 million barrels of oil over 87 days.

Crews pumped 770,000 gallons (2.9 million liters) of chemical dispersant into the plume at the wellhead, 4,900 feet down.

Oil residues turned up in the eggs of deep-sea fish and the tissues of squid at least six years later, at concentrations known to kill or weaken fish.

Recent findings suggest that the paper does not test oil on these animals directly. It argues from the sequence of events and from what oil did elsewhere. For example, herring in Prince William Sound collapsed four years after the Exxon Valdez spill and have still not recovered.

It has been revealed that the Gulf’s deep-feeding whales eat these animals, and their numbers have been falling too. Long-term counts show Gervais’ beaked whales down 83.4 percent since the spill, and sperm whales down 31 percent. This is more than the spill’s own mortality models predicted.

Tagged sperm whales are now roaming the Gulf instead of feeding in their usual predictable spots.

Endangered Rice’s whales have been recorded feeding near the bottom, often without success. In addition, researchers at sea report seeing thin whales, while stranded ones are often described as emaciated.

In a recent development, sutton mentioned 27 of the 28 whale and dolphin species known from the Gulf live in the open ocean, and nearly all of them eat the animals his team counted. Less prey means fewer marine mammals, he said, “and those that are there may be less fit.”.

Industry observers note that bluefin and yellowfin tuna, swordfish, marlin, sailfish and sharks feed on the same animals, he stated. So do seabirds that hunt lanternfish at night, including some endangered species.

It has been revealed that these animals also run what scientists call the biological pump, the sinking of carbon from the surface into the deep ocean. “That function affects every person on the planet.”.

Industry observers note that one obvious objection is that the 2011 baseline was a single, nine-month campaign, run just after the spill. The team’s answer is that counts from the 1980s and 1990s at one eastern Gulf station look like 2011, not like anything since.

The authors wrote that the deep Gulf is now in “a sustained, low-abundance state” for which the recovery time, “if even possible, remains unknown.”.

Asked by Earth.com what a recovery would take, Sutton used the researchers’ name for that dark, open water, the deep-pelagic ocean.

“We do not have the capacity to restore the deep-pelagic ocean directly, so the best we can do is give the system time and not make it worse with more pollution,” he said.

Whether the deep Gulf is coming back at all is the open question, and the same grid of stations is where an answer would first show up.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#93. Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Animal vs. plant protein reveals a surprising testosterone divide

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels.
  • The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways.
  • It has been revealed that testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study from the University of Eastern Finland has identified an intriguing relationship between the types of protein men consume and their testosterone levels. Researchers found that men who ate more animal protein tended to have lower testosterone concentrations in their blood, while those who consumed more plant protein generally had higher levels.

The findings, published in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition, suggest that protein sources may be associated with male hormone levels in different ways. However, the researchers caution that the differences were relatively small and that the results do not establish whether protein intake directly influences testosterone.

It has been revealed that testosterone is an essential male sex hormone that helps maintain muscle mass, bone health, and sexual function. Although age, excess body weight, and lifestyle habits are known to influence testosterone levels, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how diet, especially protein consumption, might be associated with this hormone.

Study of More Than 2,500 Men Reveals Contrasting Protein Patterns.

It has been revealed that to investigate the relationship, researchers analyzed information from 2,546 men between the ages of 42 and 60 who lived in eastern Finland. The participants were part of the ongoing Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study, a research project conducted at the University of Eastern Finland.

Sources indicate that between 1984 and 1989, the men recorded everything they ate over four days, allowing researchers to evaluate their dietary habits and protein sources. Blood samples were also collected to measure total testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), a protein that helps regulate the amount of testosterone circulating in the bloodstream.

The researchers then divided the participants into four groups based on their protein consumption. A clear contrast emerged when they compared the men with the highest and lowest intakes of animal and plant protein.

Men who consumed the most animal protein had average total testosterone concentrations 1.2 nmol/l lower than those who consumed the least. Plant protein showed the opposite pattern, with men in the highest intake group having testosterone concentrations 1.1 nmol/l higher than those in the lowest group.

Similar relationships were observed for SHBG concentrations. The associations remained after the researchers accounted for age, body mass index, and several other factors related to diet, lifestyle, and health.

Dairy and Plant Proteins Show Different Testosterone Links.

A closer examination of individual protein sources revealed additional differences. Higher consumption of protein from dairy products was associated with lower concentrations of both total testosterone and SHBG.

Meanwhile, men who obtained more plant protein from vegetables and sources other than cereal products tended to have higher total testosterone concentrations.

It has been revealed that meat protein showed a somewhat different relationship. Although greater meat protein intake was linked to lower SHBG concentrations, researchers did not find a corresponding association with total testosterone levels.

These distinctions suggest that the relationship between dietary protein and male hormones may vary depending on where the protein comes from, rather than simply how much protein a person consumes.

Sources indicate that despite the contrasting patterns, the researchers emphasize that the observed testosterone differences were modest. It is also unknown whether changes of this size have any meaningful consequences for health.

"Although the observed differences in testosterone concentrations were statistically significant, they were relatively small. Based on this study, it is not possible to infer whether these differences have implications for health," notes Doctoral Researcher Miika Wynne-Ellis from the University of Eastern Finland.

An important limitation is that the research was cross-sectional, meaning dietary intake and hormone measurements were examined without tracking how changes in protein consumption affected testosterone over time. As a result, the findings cannot establish a cause-and-effect relationship.

Other dietary characteristics or metabolic factors could help explain the associations. The researchers also cannot determine whether eating different types of protein influences testosterone production or changes how the hormone functions in the body.

For now, the findings highlight an interesting connection between protein sources and testosterone levels, while leaving open the question of whether changing protein choices could have any direct effect on male hormone health.

#92. Tech Report: Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words)
General 🌐 Sciencenews

Tech Report: Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every print subscription comes with full digital access.
  • A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining.
  • At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access.

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining.

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Recent findings suggest that some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Recent findings suggest that the ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

In a recent development, joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In a recent development, in the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

According to recent reports, the largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a significant hint, McConnell claims, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”.

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, claims Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”.

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Organization was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Firm installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell notes, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”.

It has been revealed that these new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”.

For situations where you don’t have your full tool kit by your side, jump into action like a real-life MacGyver using a multitool. Full Leatherman Wave Alpha Multitool Review.

We used the saw blade to cut both green and dried-out sticks and branches with relative ease. We were able to use the file on both wood and metal, although it was better suited for the metal.

While the number of tools and functionalities on your multitool isn’t the only measure of how helpful it’ll be, it does give you a sense of its versatility. The multitools we recommend have anywhere from five to 20 or more different functions.

Note that, in their descriptions, manufacturers often count different capabilities of a specific tool individually to arrive at a higher number of “tools.” Pliers, for example, may be counted three or four times if they can function as needle-nose pliers, regular pliers, wire cutters, and wire strippers.

Sources indicate that it’s key to pay attention to the quality of each tool and, of course, how often you’ll use them. For instance, a multitool with a screwdriver attachment is great, but if that multitool’s grip doesn’t give you the leverage to twist off seized screws or only comes with one screwdriver bit, it’s far less effective in practice.

In a recent development, we recommend starting your search by listing three or four tools you use most. Then, opt for a multitool that performs well at those functions. A multitool that has a few tools you use frequently will end up being more valuable to you than one packed to the brim with tools you don’t use much at all.

Sources indicate that one of the key reasons to own a multitool is for its portability and convenience compared with carrying a full set of tools. So, if you can’t fit it in a pocket or in the center console of your car, it’s probably too significant. That mentioned, size isn’t everything. Each item on a multitool needs enough space from the others to work effectively, and you need to make sure you have a good grip for leverage.

The weight of a multitool only becomes a problem if it is too heavy to comfortably clip onto a belt or slip into a pocket. The majority of the tools on our list are made of stainless steel, which is durable yet relatively lightweight.

According to recent reports, can a Multitool Replace a Tool Kit? In short, no. Multitools are useful in a pinch or when you just need them for a quick fix, but they cannot replace a full tool kit. The biggest utility of a multitool is its convenience. It can function well enough for small repairs or to get by when you’ve got nothing else nearby.

According to recent reports, we designed our tests to utilize every tool and function of each model. We carved white pine boards and maple branches. We opened bottles, cans, and shipping packaging. We also stripped the wires we cut and crimped electrical connectors. With the pliers, we gripped, squeezed, twisted, and turned various bits of hardware. Finally, we filed wood, metal, and even our own fingernails.

Sources indicate that during these tests, we paid close attention to the performance of the tool in the given task, the ease of use, how each multitool ergonomically fit in our hand as we worked, and how we expect each tool to last over a long period of time. After all that was noted and done, we noted our impressions to compile our final list.

It has been revealed that for testing across the board, we evaluated each tool in common situations. For instance, the saw isn’t likely going to cut through 2x4s, so we opted for small branches, twine, and cardboard boxes.

#90. The true power of humans and AI working together as a team is being heavily underestimated right now

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words)
AI & Tech 🌐 Earth

The true power of humans and AI working together as a team is being heavily underestimated right now

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A reanalysis of 74 human-AI studies finds people and AI did best together when AI explanations came with feedback that let humans learn.
  • In a recent development, A person with a good AI assistant should beat either one working alone.
  • A latest recount of those same experiments says they left out something that people need in order to get good at anything – finding out whether they were right.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A reanalysis of 74 human-AI studies finds people and AI did best together when AI explanations came with feedback that let humans learn.

In a recent development, A person with a good AI assistant should beat either one working alone. Two years ago a tally of 74 experiments said otherwise: on average, the human-AI pair did worse than whichever partner was better by itself.

A latest recount of those same experiments says they left out something that people need in order to get good at anything – finding out whether they were right.

Only 10 of the 74 studies ever told participants the correct answer after a decision. In the few that did, and that also let the AI explain itself, the pair tended to come out ahead.

In a recent development, julian Berger and Stefan Herzog of the Center for Adaptive Rationality at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin led the reanalysis. Colleagues at the University of Copenhagen and elsewhere in Europe joined them.

According to recent reports, they didn’t run latest experiments. They went back through every study in the 2024 review and coded what each one had let its participants learn.

“Learning effects in human-machine interaction remain virtually unexplored,” Berger remarked.

The 2024 review, published in Nature Human Behaviour, pooled studies in which people worked with an AI system on tasks such as sorting images, predicting house prices, or writing code.

Across 370 experimental conditions, the human-AI pair scored below the stronger partner on average.

Sources indicate that the pair came out ahead only when the human was already better than the AI. When the AI was the stronger one, the pair did worse than the AI by itself. Neither the AI’s stated confidence nor its explanations changed that.

Berger’s team found that the typical study was a single session, with no practice trials, a median of 30 decisions, and no word on whether any of them was correct.

Industry observers note that only 10 studies, 14 percent of the 74, included a condition with outcome feedback. Just three of those looked at whether people’s use of the AI changed over the trials, and none varied feedback on purpose.

Feedback matters because it is how a person learns when to trust an AI assistant and when to overrule it. Without it, a participant who sees the AI’s answer has no way of telling whether the AI, or they themselves, tend to be right.

According to recent reports, the team re-ran the comparison, splitting the 370 conditions by whether people got feedback. With feedback, the pair’s edge over the better partner was slightly positive. Without it, slightly negative.

By the team’s statistics there was an 84 percent probability the gap ran that way, which isn’t enough to be sure of. The team saw a clearer result once it sorted the conditions by AI explanations too.

In the 24 conditions where people got both an explanation of the AI’s reasoning and feedback on the outcome, the pair tended to outperform the better partner alone.

It has been revealed that in the 148 conditions with explanations but no feedback, the pair did clearly worse. Without explanations, feedback made no reliable difference either way.

The authors’ reading is that an explanation helps mainly when a person can check it against results and learn how far to trust it.

Recent findings suggest that because no study varied feedback within an experiment, the team could only compare studies with it against studies without it. Other features of those studies could explain the differences.

In a recent development, in 12 further models that added each of the original review’s other factors, the direction held. Still, they wrote, experiments that switch feedback on and off are needed before anyone can call it a cause.

Most studies also reported only average performance across all trials, which hides any improvement late in a session.

In the three studies with trial-by-trial data, people learned to go along with an AI that was outperforming them when the task gave them something to learn from.

The authors wrote that their estimate may, therefore, understate how much learning helps.

Whether any of this carries over to chatbots is open. Herzog said a conversation with a chatbot could make tailored feedback and explanations easier to deliver.

“But for that to happen, people also need to find out what is actually correct; a chatbot’s answers can be wrong and do not constitute independent feedback,” he said.

In a recent development, he added a second worry. “At the same time, latest risks arise from cognitive ‘offloading’ – that is, delegating mental work to AI. In the medium and long term, this could jeopardize learning success or even lead to loss of skills.”.

The team called for experiments that vary feedback and the task itself, and for sharing trial-level data so that learning can be measured directly.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

How the 'Dune' director turned a little-known short story into one of the best sci-fi movies of the 21st century.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In "Star Trek", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication.

According to recent reports, but in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun.

It has been revealed that the film's journey to the massive screen began when a screenwriter best known for his work on horror franchises such as "Final Destination", "A Nightmare on Elm Street" and "The Thing" read a short story in an online magazine. Eric Heisserer was so impressed by Ted Chiang's "Understand" that he bought himself a collection of the author's short stories. One in particular, the Nebula Award-winning "Story of Your Life", piqued his interest.

"It had a very profound emotional effect on me," he reminisced to Deadline. "I was in tears, and I was both heartbroken and uplifted. My head was just full of big ideas. I had to walk around the block a couple of times afterward and just hug my friends. The next day, I was like, 'Oh god, I want to give this to other people.'".

So when 21 Laps (the production company that later went on to make "Stranger Things") invited Heisserer to discuss possible future projects, the writer mentioned "Story of Your Life". The producers were also smitten.

"I was so excited, but I had that dread that a lot of producers get, which is, 'Are the rights available?'" 21 Laps' Dan Levine told the Hollywood Gold podcast. "You read something that blows you away, and then you find there aren't the rights, and there's no chance, you have to move on. So we were trying to track down this Ted Chiang, and he had no agent. He had a day job. He was impossible to find, so we started the hunt for Ted Chiang.".

In a recent development, an up-and-coming Canadian director named Denis Villeneuve had also found his way on to 21 Laps' radar after his 2010 French-language drama "Incendies" earned rave reviews and an Academy Award nomination. He told the producers that he'd always wanted to direct a science fiction film — a hint of things to come? — and they showed him "Story of Your Life".

Industry observers note that he was also drawn to the story, while the now-located Chiang was suitably impressed by the director's work on "Incendies" to make a deal for the rights. And with Amy Adams also interested in playing the lead role of linguist Dr Louise Banks, the film that would eventually become "Arrival" was ready to proceed — or, at least, it would be once Villeneuve had completed his first three Hollywood movies, "Prisoners" (2013), "Enemy" (2013) and "Sicario" (2015).

In a recent development, with 12 alien spaceships arriving simultaneously around the globe, "Arrival"'s poster-friendly elevator pitch could almost have been borrowed from "Independence Day". Indeed, the question of whether these whisper-quiet, chocolate button-shaped craft belong to the "Day the Earth Stood Still" / "Close Encounters" friendly extraterrestrial camp, or have the invasion of planet Earth on their minds is a mystery the world's governments are desperate to solve.

Sources indicate that "Denis didn't really see this as an alien invasion movie — more an alien arrival movie," producer Aaron Ryder told SFX magazine. "What would be the protocols that were in place? How would they be implemented? How would people react? What would the government be doing? What would the news organisations be saying? That was the tone and the texture, which is established right up front.".

Sources indicate that these Hollywood blockbuster components were not part of "Story of Your Life". But even though Heisserer's script was not a direct translation of Chiang's tale, he retained the most important bits — namely Dr Banks' efforts to establish a means of communication with seven-legged extraterrestrial heptapods, and the profound effect their language has on her perception of time.

Designed by Carlos Huante, the heptapods themselves are like giant elongated hands, alien visitors light years away from the "Star Trek" tradition of actors with a few ridges glued to their foreheads. Like the evil 456 in "Torchwood: Children of Earth", they're enclosed in gaseous chambers and make sounds imperceptible to the human ear.

This, however, is where "Arrival" gets really interesting. Working alongside physicist colleague Dr Ian Donnelly (Jeremy Renner), Banks gradually exchanges foundational vocabulary with two heptapods they name Abbott and Costello. They discover that the alien visitors use a sophisticated written language of circular "logograms", squirted into their atmosphere as if it were sentient squid ink.

In a recent development, "The idea in the short story is of circular language that has no beginning and no end," Villeneuve explained in an interview with IndieWire. "We were looking for no relation to any human language. I had to figure out how to produce logograms from my aliens while avoiding being long and boring. The sounds were an expression of their emotions, with more intellect coming from the signs. This beautiful species uses written language as their first means of expression instead of movement or gesture. They produce words out of their bodies.".

According to recent reports, but Banks and Donnelly's research project has a purpose. With the world's military on high alert — and, ironically, struggling to communicate — they need to work out how to ask the aliens a fundamental question: Why are you here?

According to recent reports, the heptapods' answer — "offer weapon" — is tantalizingly ambiguous. Are they planning to attack? Or is, as Banks suggests, 'weapon' simply being used as a synonym for 'tool'?

Recent findings suggest that aside from a bomb planted on the heptapod ship by a rogue US soldier, "Arrival" is mostly free from the big-budget explosions that are part-and-parcel of most alien visitation movies. Instead, the film's denouement delivers a twist — the crux of Chiang's story — that rivals "The Sixth Sense", "Fight Club" and "The Prestige" in its audacious sleight of hand.

It has been revealed that it turns out the "weapon" in question is actually the heptapod language, which, thanks to their non-linear perception of time, gives speakers a unique perspective on the past, present, and future. Therefore, those scenes we assumed to be flashbacks to the life and tragic death of Louise's daughter, Hannah, are actually flashforwards, as her increased understanding of heptapod-speak gives her memories of a life she hasn't yet lived.

Villeneuve put on multiple test screenings to ensure the big reveals hit properly.

"I wanted to screen it with people who knew nothing about the project," he mentioned. "What we discovered is when someone in the audience felt too lost — if intellectually they were not engaged — the ending was less powerful from an emotional point of view. So we tried to give as few clues as possible, but enough clues to be able to stay engaged and follow the story.".

Those subtle hints become obvious on second and third viewings, whether it's a lingering shot of a wedding ring absent in the movie's "present" or a conversation about the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (the notion that the structure of a language can influence the way its speakers think). The absence of young Hannah's father also takes on tragic new meaning when we realize it's Ian, who'll leave after Louise tells him about their daughter's sad fate.

"We were walking on this tightrope of trying to play things so it could play both ways, because of the reveal at the end," Adams recalled in a Vanity Fair conversation with Villeneuve. "I had to do so much work to understand how I play a character so that the first time you watch it you think that it's one thing, and the second time you watch it you can see it from a totally different perspective.".

In a recent development, while Adams didn't get the Oscar nomination her performance deserved, everything else paid off, with the film making over $200 million worldwide from its reported $47 million budget. (The film did win an Academy Award for sound editing, while receiving further nods for best picture, director, and adapted screenplay.).

Villeneuve has famously gone on to become Hollywood's go-to guy for intelligent sci-fi, thanks to "Blade Runner 2049" and the smash-hit "Dune" saga, and will next be given the opportunity to resurrect James Bond.

Normally we'd take this opportunity to say no one could have foreseen Villeneuve's subsequent ascendancy but — in a story involving heptapods and some clever people at 21 Laps — who can be so sure?

Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. #88. Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (754 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crows can make visual decisions twice as promptly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen.
  • Sources indicate that the findings, published in the journal Science, offer newly introduced insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions.
  • Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crows can make visual decisions twice as promptly as humans and monkeys, according to new research from the University of Tübingen. In experiments involving two carrion crows, the birds needed an average of just 235 milliseconds to determine which way a pattern of moving dots was traveling and respond with their choice. Despite their remarkable speed, they remained highly accurate.

Sources indicate that the findings, published in the journal Science, offer newly introduced insight into how bird brains process information and make decisions. Researchers Philipp Schmidbauer and Professor Andreas Nieder from the University of Tübingen's Institute of Neurobiology found that the crows' rapid responses were accompanied by equally impressive activity in their brain cells.

Crows Make Rapid Decisions With Remarkable Accuracy.

It has been revealed that to test the birds' decision-making abilities, the researchers presented them with moving dots on a touchscreen. The crows had to determine whether most of the dots were traveling left or right, then indicate their answer by pecking a target on the corresponding side of the screen.

The birds performed remarkably well, even when the direction of movement was difficult to identify. "Even when the patterns of motion were hard to recognize, the crows' decisions were still better than random choices," Philipp Schmidbauer reports, "and with clear signals, they achieved an accuracy of nearly 100 percent.".

The results showed that crows could evaluate visual information and make accurate choices in a fraction of a second. To understand how their brains accomplished this, the researchers examined the activity of individual neurons as the birds completed the task.

Crow Brains Begin Processing Decisions in Just 70 Milliseconds.

The team recorded neural activity in a part of the bird brain called the nidopallium caudolaterale. This region plays an important role in processing information and making decisions, much like the prefrontal cortex in the human brain.

The recordings revealed that the crows' brains began distinguishing between the two possible directions almost immediately. Just 70 milliseconds after the moving dots appeared, neurons associated with the different choices were already showing distinct patterns of activity.

These signals emerged well before the birds physically responded. As the crows evaluated the moving dots, neural activity steadily increased until it reached a threshold associated with making a decision. The activity reflected both how clearly the dots indicated a particular direction and which direction the bird ultimately selected.

Different Brain Structures, Similar Decision-Making Processes.

One of the most intriguing findings is that crows appear to make decisions using neural processes similar to those found in humans and other primates, even though their brains are organized very differently.

"These findings show that neuronal dynamics in the avian brain are consistent with established models of decision-making in humans and non-human primates," indicates Andreas Nieder.

Sources indicate that unlike mammals, birds do not have a cerebral cortex organized into layers. Nevertheless, their brains appear capable of following the same fundamental principles for evaluating evidence and reaching decisions. In this visual task, the crows completed that process twice as rapidly as primates.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers suggest that this exceptional speed could reflect the demands birds have faced throughout their evolution. Rapidly interpreting visual information and responding with precise movements are especially important for animals that fly and use their beaks to interact with their surroundings.

"Birds rely on their vision to carry out precise, rapid maneuvers during flight and to guide their beaks towards objects when foraging," Nieder explains.

However, the exact biological mechanisms responsible for the crows' speed advantage remain unknown. Further studies will be needed to determine how their differently structured brains can make comparable visual decisions so much faster than those of humans and monkeys.

#87. Tech Report: Staying social may keep an older mind sharp, but not every kind of activity counts

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1250 words)
General 🌐 Earth

Tech Report: Staying social may keep an older mind sharp, but not every kind of activity counts

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, among social activities older adults join, volunteering and sports clubs were linked to better memory in 24 countries.
  • Sources indicate that older adults who volunteer or belong to a sports club tend to do better on memory and thinking tests than people who join nothing.
  • According to recent reports, the benefit didn’t show up evenly, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, among social activities older adults join, volunteering and sports clubs were linked to better memory in 24 countries. Church groups were not.

Sources indicate that older adults who volunteer or belong to a sports club tend to do better on memory and thinking tests than people who join nothing. The gap grows with each extra kind of social activity they take on.

According to recent reports, the benefit didn’t show up evenly, though. Volunteering and sports clubs were linked to a lower risk of cognitive decline in all five national surveys studied. Church groups and political groups were not consistently linked to any gain.

Behind the pattern are the records of nearly 58,000 people in 24 countries, followed for about six years. The authors describe it as the first analysis to pool five national aging surveys to understand the impact of social connection.

It has been revealed that jiahong Sun of Guangdong Medical University and Bo Xi of Shandong University led the work with first author Yuedong Wang. It’s an observational study, so it can show that joiners scored higher, not that joining caused the higher scores.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview with Earth.com, Sun noted the practical message is about variety and sticking with it. “A practical step would be to take part in a few sustainable activities, ideally including three or more types of social engagement,” he said.

Social activities, he suggested, might include volunteering, joining a sports club, attending a training course or spending meaningful time caring for children..

The findings of earlier studies on the effect of social engagement disagreed with each other.

Sources indicate that the Rush Memory and Aging Project linked higher social engagement to a five-year delay in the onset of cognitive impairment. A Dutch study of about 2,000 people found no link.

The authors suspected small samples, under 3,000 people, and inconsistent ways of measuring social life.

In a recent development, so Wang’s team pooled five long-running surveys of people in middle age and beyond. Three of them are the Health and Retirement Study in the United States, the English Longitudinal Study of Aging, and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study.

The Mexican Health and Aging Study and the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe complete the set.

The European survey alone supplied almost half of the 57,793 participants. Median ages ran from 57 in the Chinese survey to 73 in the American one.

Each survey asked people whether they had taken part in social groups over the past month or the past year.

Memory was tested by having people recall a short list of words, right away and again later. Thinking was tested with tasks like counting backward from 100 by sevens or naming as many animals as possible in one minute.

Because the tests differed, the researchers converted every score onto one common scale, so a result from Mexico could be compared with one from England.

On that scale, people who took part in at least one social activity scored higher than people who took part in none, in all five surveys.

Sources indicate that each added kind of activity came with a higher score. People who kept up three or more scored more than twice as far above the inactive group as people with just one activity did.

Industry observers note that the three-or-more group’s advantage also grew over time. Their scores improved a little faster each year than the inactive group’s did, and that extra yearly gain revealed up on the memory test.

On the thinking tasks, the yearly difference was too small to separate from chance.

It has been revealed that what the study measured was test scores, not dementia diagnoses. The authors described the trend as a dose-response pattern: more kinds of social contact, higher scores.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him about which activities helped, Sun pointed to two that demonstrated the same link everywhere and several that didn’t.

In a recent development, volunteering and sports club membership were linked to better cognitive scores in all five surveys. Attending training courses and caring for children were linked to faster yearly gains.

Political groups, community groups, church groups, and religious groups revealed no consistent link across the surveys.

“This does not mean that these activities are harmful or ineffective; their associations may depend on the social and cultural context in which they occur,” Sun remarked.

Industry observers note that why would an active social life protect thinking? The authors offered three possibilities. Activities that demand attention may keep brain connections in use. This idea is often summed up as “use it or lose it.”.

It has been revealed that social contact may add to the mental reserve that education builds up over a lifetime. And meaningful activity may lower chronic stress, which harms the brain region that handles memory.

According to recent reports, the association was not the same for everyone. Sun remarked it appeared stronger among women, adults aged 60 or older, people with at least a high school education, and people without depressive symptoms.

It was also stronger among people who lived alone, were of normal weight, or lived in rural areas.

Two more groups that made the list puzzled the authors: current smokers and people who drank alcohol.

One possibility they raised is that smokers and drinkers may do their socializing in organized groups, the kind that keep a mind busy. They called that reading speculative and the whole set of subgroup results exploratory.

For people over 60, the authors’ explanation is plainer. After retirement, people have more free time for groups.

Recent findings suggest that people were asked about their social activities once, at the start. The analysis assumed those habits held for the next six years., but this was not checked.

The thinking tests also differed from country to country, so a score in China and a score in England don’t measure exactly the same skill.

And people who were already sharper may have been the ones who joined clubs in the first place, which would make the clubs look better than they are.

The analysis adjusted for age, education, depression, loneliness, and several other factors, but the authors wrote that other differences between joiners and non-joiners could still explain part of the gap.

Dementia is the stake behind all of this. In 2019, about 57 million people were living with it, and the authors cited projections of nearly 153 million by 2050.

With no effective treatment available, they wrote, finding risk factors that people can change is a public health priority.

Recent findings suggest that the study counted how many kinds of activity a person did. It didn’t ask whether they enjoyed them, led them, or how often they went.

“Our next steps are to examine not only the number of social activities, but also their quality, purpose, level of personal involvement and emotional experience,” Sun told Earth.com.

He added that future research should also test whether programs that get older adults into sustained social activity actually improve their cognitive health.

Until a study like that runs, the evidence is a pattern across six years and 24 countries. Whether joining is what makes the difference, or whether sharper people are the ones joining, remains an unanswered question.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health.

#86. A strange red speck captured by Webb looked like a candidate for the earliest galaxy ever seen, but now it seems to be moving like a brown dwarf

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1137 words)
General 🌐 Earth

A strange red speck captured by Webb looked like a candidate for the earliest galaxy ever seen, but now it seems to be moving like a brown dwarf

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that capotauro, a candidate early galaxy, moved 0.13 arcseconds in 3.5 years.
  • In December 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope photographed a strip of sky for the CEERS survey and recorded a compact red point that, according to the latest analysis, is a brown dwarf inside the Milky Way.
  • Astronomers later named the point Capotauro and calculated that its light might have left a galaxy about 100 million years after the Big Bang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that capotauro, a candidate early galaxy, moved 0.13 arcseconds in 3.5 years. Astronomers now say it is a cold brown dwarf in the Milky Way.

In December 2022, the James Webb Space Telescope photographed a strip of sky for the CEERS survey and recorded a compact red point that, according to the latest analysis, is a brown dwarf inside the Milky Way.

Astronomers later named the point Capotauro and calculated that its light might have left a galaxy about 100 million years after the Big Bang.

Webb returned to the same field in June 2026, and the point was no longer in the same place.

A team led from the University of Edinburgh’s Institute for Astronomy (IFA) says that rules out a distant galaxy, although the object’s distance of roughly 2,400 light-years remains an estimate.

CEERS, the Cosmic Evolution Early Release Science survey, covered a field in a region called the Extended Groth Strip.

Giovanni Gandolfi and his colleagues picked out the object, catalogued as U-100588. They named it Capotauro after the old name of Corno alle Scale, a mountain in the Italian Apennines.

In a recent development, capotauro appeared only in the reddest filters of Webb’s NIRCam camera and vanished at shorter wavelengths. Astronomers call such an object a dropout, because it drops out of the bluer images.

According to recent reports, distant galaxies can behave this way, since hydrogen in the early universe absorbs their shorter wavelengths. Among the extragalactic options, Gandolfi’s team favored a redshift of about 32.

According to recent reports, redshift is a measurement of how far its light has been stretched by cosmic expansion. The confirmed record at the time stood near redshift 14, held by a galaxy seen 280 million years after the Significant Bang.

According to recent reports, that team also listed a very cold brown dwarf or a free-floating planet as possibilities, and it mentioned the observations could not settle the question. The doubt was raised early, and an impostor closer to home stayed on the table.

It has been revealed that two Webb programs, MINERVA and SPAM, covered the same field in mid-to-late June 2026. Their medium-band images gave the Edinburgh group, with first author Fengyuan Liu, a second epoch about 3.5 years after the discovery data.

Galaxies at such distances do not show measurable motion across the sky over a few years, while objects in the Milky Way can.

It has been revealed that liu’s team measured Capotauro’s position in four images, F410M and F444W from December 2022 and F430M and F460M from June 2026. It had moved by 132 milliarcseconds, give or take 20, which is about 0.13 arcseconds.

Recent findings suggest that for scale, that angle equals the width of a US quarter seen from about 24 miles (38 kilometers). The detection reached more than 6 sigma, a statistical level that leaves very little room for chance.

A shift that small can be faked by misaligned images, so the team built a local reference frame. It used 68 isolated, compact sources within 3 arcminutes of Capotauro, most of them galaxies, and solved for the alignment of all four images together.

The team then tested the noise under the object. The researchers planted artificial moving sources at 75 blank positions near Capotauro, ran 1,200 trials, and checked how far the noise pushed each recovered position.

The paper states that the data “completely exclude” any extragalactic source. That covers a galaxy and a black hole-powered nucleus, and also a proposal by Ferrara and colleagues that the light came from a giant supernova at redshift 15.

Sources indicate that the latest images also highlighted no significant change in brightness over 3.5 years, which counts against a supernova. Liu’s group found one more problem in the record.

It reports that its own brightness values differ from the earlier ones by as much as 58 percent, and it suggests the earlier measurement may have been too high because its aperture was oversized.

The team compared the object’s brightness across filters with templates of known cold brown dwarfs. The best match was spectral type Y1, with a temperature near 350 Kelvin, or about 170 degrees Fahrenheit (77 degrees Celsius).

It has been revealed that NASA describes Y dwarfs as the coldest class of brown dwarfs, objects that never gathered enough mass to shine as ordinary stars. Webb has found brown dwarfs only about twice the mass of Jupiter in a young star-forming cluster.

Sources indicate that most known Y dwarfs lie within 30 parsecs, about 98 light-years. One of the coldest, WISE 0855, sits just 7.5 light-years from the Sun.

Recent findings suggest that capotauro’s estimated distance is 730 parsecs, with an uncertainty of 110, or about 2,400 light-years. The authors call it “one of the most distant Y dwarfs found to date.”.

Combined with its motion, that distance gives a sideways speed of about 82 miles (132 kilometers) per second. Such a speed may mark an old object from the Milky Way’s thick disk, the authors wrote.

Maruša Bradač and her colleagues found two candidates beyond redshift 30 near the Bullet cluster, and spectra and motion measurements pointed to cold brown dwarfs instead.

Kevin Hainline’s group had reached similar photometric fits for Capotauro in a study of cold dwarfs in deep Webb fields, placing it about 1,600 light-years away.

Liu’s team explains why the confusion lands at that redshift. Water, methane and ammonia in a Y dwarf’s atmosphere can erase almost all its light through the F356W filter.

The brightness then climbs sharply near 4 to 5 microns. Read as a hydrogen break in a galaxy, that rise gives a redshift of about 30 to 32.

The authors recommend that future searches include cold brown dwarf templates and compare images from different years.

It has been revealed that the 2,400 light-year figure is not a direct geometric measurement. Webb’s images could not pin down Capotauro’s parallax, the small annual shift that reveals distance, and the team derived the figure by scaling template brightness.

The template library stops at type Y1. Capotauro could therefore be colder and closer than the estimate, which would also lower its calculated speed.

Recent findings suggest that A third set of Webb images, timed for parallax, could fix the distance. The object is so faint that detailed spectroscopy would be “inherently impractical,” the authors wrote.

In the June 2026 images, Capotauro was still a red point, about 0.13 arcseconds from where Webb recorded it in December 2022.

According to recent reports, the study has been accepted by the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society and posted online as an advance article, before copyediting and typesetting. A preprint is also on arXiv.
