#85. A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words)
AI & Tech 🌐 Sciencedaily

A breakthrough in magnetism could make AI chips use dramatically less energy

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A promising latest approach to building computer chips could dramatically reduce the energy needed for computing, including the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence.
  • These materials could make future electronics far more energy efficient than today's technology.
  • In a recent development, researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A promising latest approach to building computer chips could dramatically reduce the energy needed for computing, including the rapidly growing demands of artificial intelligence. At the center of the breakthrough is a special class of materials known as multiferroics, which combine electrical and magnetic properties that can be controlled together using extremely small voltages.

These materials could make future electronics far more energy efficient than today's technology. However, a major obstacle has prevented their use in conventional computer chips. When multiferroics are made thin enough to fit inside these devices, they typically lose the electrical and magnetic behavior that makes them valuable. Scientists call this problem the "dead layer" effect.

In a recent development, researchers at Brown University have now developed a way to overcome this limitation. Their technique produces extremely thin films of bismuth ferrite, a widely studied multiferroic material, without sacrificing its essential properties. Even more remarkably, the process gives the material new magnetic characteristics that could make it especially useful for future electronics.

According to recent reports, "We've established that we can get rid of the dead layer," noted Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown who led the work. "We show that you can make this material basically as thin as you want -- down to a few angstroms -- and it's still ferroelectric, and it's still magnetic.".

The findings were published in the journal Nature Materials.

Why Multiferroics Could Transform Computer Chips.

What makes multiferroics so attractive for computing is the unusual connection between their electrical and magnetic properties. Their atomic structure is made up of repeating units in which positive and negative charges are positioned on opposite sides, creating a property known as electrical polarization.

In a recent development, applying a small voltage can reverse this polarization, effectively switching the positions of the positive and negative charges. This provides a potential way to store digital information as binary values (ones and zeros) using very little electricity.

Because the material's magnetic behavior is linked to its electrical polarization, the stored information can also be retrieved magnetically. This combination could enable computer memory and logic components that require significantly less energy than existing technologies.

The challenge has been making these materials small enough for practical devices. Modern computer chips require exceptionally thin layers, but multiferroics traditionally stop functioning properly when reduced to such dimensions.

Two separate effects cause this breakdown. First, the material's atomic structure becomes distorted, disrupting the arrangement and chemical environment necessary for its properties to function. Second, internal electric fields interfere with the material's polarization until it can no longer be maintained. Together, these effects destroy both its ferroelectric and magnetic behavior, creating the troublesome dead layer.

How Brown Engineers Eliminated the Dead Layer.

To solve the problem, the Brown University team developed a new method for producing thin films of bismuth ferrite.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers deposited the material onto a foundation made of dysprosium scandate, a compound derived from rare earth elements. This underlying material has a crystal structure with slightly smaller dimensions than bismuth ferrite, creating a mismatch between their atomic arrangements.

That mismatch places the bismuth ferrite under compression, helping preserve the atomic structure required for its electrical and magnetic properties to remain intact.

The team also incorporated a second metallic layer designed to counteract unwanted electric fields. By preventing those fields from disrupting the material's electrical polarization, the additional layer addresses the other major cause of the dead layer effect.

Together, these changes allow the bismuth ferrite film to retain its multiferroic properties even when reduced to just a few angstroms in thickness.

It has been revealed that but the researchers discovered something else. Rather than simply preserving the material's original capabilities, their approach actually improved its magnetic behavior.

The engineered layers caused the bismuth ferrite to exhibit altermagnetism, an unusual form of magnetism that combines useful characteristics of two more familiar magnetic states: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism.

This discovery could be particularly crucial for developing faster and more compact computer components.

It has been revealed that "Ferromagnets are useful for memory and logic because they produce strong magnetic signals that are easy to read out," Caretta said. "The challenge is that they are relatively slow, and their stray magnetic fields make it difficult to pack devices densely on a chip without interference. Antiferromagnets can operate much faster and avoid those stray fields, but their signals are much harder to detect. Altermagnets are kind of the best of both worlds -- they can be fast, densely integrated and still provide a strong electrical signal for readout.".

According to recent reports, in other words, altermagnets offer a potentially valuable combination of speed, compactness, and readable signals. These characteristics could help engineers build computer components that operate efficiently without the interference problems associated with conventional magnetic materials.

The ability to create this magnetic behavior in an exceptionally thin multiferroic film makes the discovery especially promising for future chip designs.

A Latest Path Toward Energy-Efficient AI Computing.

As artificial intelligence continues to drive demand for computing power, developing hardware that consumes less electricity has become an increasingly notable goal.

It has been revealed that caretta believes the fresh findings could help bring multiferroic materials closer to practical use in low-power memory and computing devices. Although the technology still needs further development before it can be incorporated into commercial chips, the research demonstrates that a long-standing materials limitation can be overcome.

Sources indicate that it also indicates that carefully engineering a material's atomic environment can do more than preserve its existing properties. Under the right conditions, it can produce useful behavior that was not present in the original material.

"We know the underlying properties are already there in the bulk materials," Caretta remarked. "The trick is learning how to engineer them into a form that's useful -- and sometimes even better than what nature gives us.".

According to recent reports, the research received funding from the U.S. Army Research Office (W911NF-21-2-0162), the National Science Foundation (DMR-2039380, OIA-2327352) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-AC02-05CH11231).

Sources indicate that scientists are racing to restore people’s ability to communicate. Powerful AI-based methods to decode speech signals and predict words, along with advances in technology, promise success.

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me takes listeners through the breadth of scientific efforts to restore words, emotions and even gestures to people who can’t move or talk.

Recent findings suggest that we’ll hear from Casey Harrell, a man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis who can no longer talk. A user of today’s technology, Harrell has a unique perspective on what he’d like to see improved for the technology of tomorrow.

#82. Which science-fiction novels have been best at predicting the future?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1690 words)
General 🌐 Newscientist

Which science-fiction novels have been best at predicting the future?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Newscientist

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Check your subscription status, update your details and more.
  • Industry observers note that newly introduced Scientist has always been interested in science fiction and its attempts to imagine the future.
  • In a recent development, it’s true that some of the sci-fi he was reading then was rapidly overtaken by events and, in the process of that, rendered redundant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check your subscription status, update your details and more.

Industry observers note that newly introduced Scientist has always been interested in science fiction and its attempts to imagine the future. In 1958, when the magazine was 2 years old, it published an article by Ian S. Menzies in which he wrote: “Like every other form of literature, s. f. ranges from excellent to awful. But the best of science fiction today is far superior to much other fiction.” Elsewhere in the feature, Menzies talked about the risks of the “rapid catching up of reality with fiction”.

In a recent development, it’s true that some of the sci-fi he was reading then was rapidly overtaken by events and, in the process of that, rendered redundant. What Menzies couldn’t know was that other works from that same period would still be regarded as prescient, notable or relevant, or even all three, decades later.

According to recent reports, so, which sci-fi stories, published over the seven decades of New Scientist’s history, have proved to be both prophetic and enduringly pertinent as the world has changed around them? Here are some of my personal picks.

Industry observers note that the Death of Grass by John Christopher (1956) is an English period piece, with all the particular social politics of its era on display (sexism included). Yet somehow it manages to foreshadow a host of modern-day crises, from pandemics and the fragility of food supply lines to the befouling and stripping of the land by substantial agriculture.

According to recent reports, the book opens with the news that a virus is killing grasses; eventually that comes to include all cereal crops. Abruptly, the country’s food reserves are gone, and no more food is coming. The novel’s main characters are mostly middle-class professionals who do a few things “right” early on. They are quick to acquire guns and flee London; also, quick to gun down anyone who tries to stop them. They make their way in convoy through a brown land, heading towards a Cumbrian valley where one of their group has a relative. The valley is gated; one way in, one way out. They think they could be safe there.

First they have to survive their journey, though, and England, within hours, is lawless. I finished the book wishing that I could buy a remote valley and build a wall across the bottom of it.

Industry observers note that the Moon Is a Harsh Mistress by Robert A. Heinlein (1966) is the story, set in 2075, of a group of lunar residents who plot to overthrow their overlords on Earth. It’s a great premise rendered quite dull in execution; much of the book reads like the minutes from a local council meeting. In addition, the sexual politics of the colony are filtered through male 1960s sensibilities, adding cringeworthy moments.

Sources indicate that the reason this remains a classic is that one of the characters in the book, Mike, is an AI. Not just some 60s idea of what an AI might be, but our idea of an AI. On the very first page, our narrator Mannie (who speaks a futuristic version of English) writes: “Mike was a fair dinkum thinkum, sharpest computer you’ll ever meet… Not that Mike would necessarily give right answer; he wasn’t completely honest.” Remind you of anything?

Ursula K. Le Guin’s astonishing novel The Dispossessed (1974) remains daisy fresh. Le Guin, as her fans will know, could do it all: character, politics, ideas, exquisite writing… and, in this case, spaceships too.

Industry observers note that our hero, Shevek, is a brilliant physicist and also a good man (what a wonderful creation he is!) trying to do right in a future where the human colonies have gone different ways – one into anarchy, for example, another into the rule of an elite – as they struggle with climate change, moral exhaustion, repression, inequality… and much else that we struggle with today. If you’ve never read this one, I highly recommend it.

I’m going to cheat for the 80s and pick two books, because I can’t choose between Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale (1985) and William Gibson’s Neuromancer (1984).

Recent findings suggest that in Atwood’s masterwork, the US has been captured by a radical right-wing group and is now called the Republic of Gilead. Women’s rights have been scrapped. Our hero, named Offred by the latest regime, is assigned as a handmaid to a family of loyalists. Her job is to produce a baby for the commander who is her new master. She is, in short, a womb with arms and legs, and nothing more, to Gilead.

I don’t think I need to draw any lines for you, straight or otherwise, from this book written 40 years ago to current events.

Atwood aside, I didn’t want to leave out Neuromancer because its vision of our digital future is so weirdly prescient. Gibson, famously, was no computer expert and wrote the book on a typewriter. Yet he foresaw what cyberspace would actually be like.

Case, our chief protagonist, is a former hacker trying to make ends meet in Japan after his ability to access cyberspace has been taken from him. Then a woman called Molly approaches him, asking him to get involved in a heist. Cue a high-stakes drama in and out of cyberspace. The book is a bit dense to start with, but it’s well worth sticking with.

Is Neuromancer’s cyberpunk dystopia still thrilling in 2025?

Industry observers note that octavia E. Butler’s Parable of the Sower (1993) is a barnstormer of a novel that remains as relevant today as when it was first published. Our hero, Lauren Olamina, is a young woman living in a gated community in a United States that is rapidly falling apart.

Climate change is escalating and the streets are full of desperate people forced into savagery simply to survive. Lauren’s community is hanging on, but soon the chaos is going to come through that gate.

Industry observers note that lauren, still a teenager, develops her own religion and names it Earthseed. Its divine purpose is for humans to colonise the stars. Such a bold vision is preposterous amidst the horror of the world Lauren is forced to make her way through, and yet it sustains her.

According to recent reports, N.K. Jemisin on the prescience and brilliance of Parable of the Sower.

The book is a hymn (I think) to the power of taking full responsibility for your life and facing up to the fact that everything changes. Let us hope, as with The Death of Grass, that this version of the future remains in some parts fictional.

Butler wrote a follow-up, Parable of the Talents, in which Lauren sees her dreams begin to come true. A third book in the series remained unfinished when Butler died.

Industry observers note that one does need some time to pass before being able to decide if a book has truly got the future right. However, I am reasonably confident that The Three-Body Problem by Cixin Liu (2008) is going to prove to be so.

3 Body Problem review: Cixin Liu’s masterpiece arrives on Netflix.

The story is a brilliant one. Aliens are heading for Earth, and they’re not friendly, but it’s going to take them hundreds of years to arrive. Can the scientists of Earth band together and push science forward so hard that humans will survive the coming invasion? Yes, Liu wrote a book all about physics, but made it gripping!

Sources indicate that so, in the case of the book, the science push is all about aliens. But it doesn’t take a significant leap of the imagination to suggest that there might be some key real world parallels here. This is the first of a trilogy. The two follow-up novels are also fantastic.

I’m going to take a chance on two very different novels from recent times that might, in the future, be viewed as accurate visions.

First, Station Eleven (2014) by Emily St. John Mandel, which essentially predicted the covid-19 pandemic. Except in Mandel’s pandemic, the world was left in ruins.

According to recent reports, we follow a travelling group of actors and musicians as they journey between communities in this future world. The book explores the idea that “survival is insufficient”; that humanity needs art, culture and history to truly live. Its ideas still feel extremely relevant 12 years later.

Sources indicate that second, Kim Stanley Robinson’s chronicle of the near future, The Ministry for the Future (2020). Clear-eyed, but essentially optimistic, it describes humanity’s efforts to deal with climate change in the decades to come.

This is a very untraditional book in structure, and although you could say the main character is Mary Murphy, the head of the titular ministry, parts of the book are devoted to (fictional) witness accounts of future events. It’s not an easy read, but then it’s not an easy subject, and this is a massively ambitious work.

Despite the horrors contained in the book, we may end up wishing, in the future, that it had been more prescient, rather than less.

So those are my picks. You may have better ones. In terms of Ian S. Menzies’s central argument seven long decades ago, I think that what he stated still holds true. Science fiction continues to range from excellent to awful. But the best of sci-fi today is still far superior to much other fiction. It’s where the major ideas are, simple as that.

Industry observers note that did Emily get it right? Come and join the discussion about the sci-fi novels that have best predicted the future.

#81. A tourist’s vacation photo of a yellow flower helped botanists catalog a completely new species

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (866 words)
General 🌐 Earth

A tourist’s vacation photo of a yellow flower helped botanists catalog a completely new species

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh yellow-flowered plant species discovered through an iNaturalist photo in Portugal's Algarve faces threats from invasive trees and habitat loss.
  • A yellow toadflax that grows almost only in the hills of Monchique, in Portugal’s Algarve region, has been described as a latest species, Linaria alfercensis.
  • It has been revealed that botanists first noticed it in a photo that a visitor to the area posted on iNaturalist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh yellow-flowered plant species discovered through an iNaturalist photo in Portugal's Algarve faces threats from invasive trees and habitat loss.

A yellow toadflax that grows almost only in the hills of Monchique, in Portugal’s Algarve region, has been described as a latest species, Linaria alfercensis.

It has been revealed that botanists first noticed it in a photo that a visitor to the area posted on iNaturalist. The citizen science platform lets people share pictures of wild plants and animals.

João Farminhão of the University of Coimbra’s Centre for Functional Ecology (CFE) described the species in August 2026 with four colleagues from Portugal and Spain. Its flowers “did not match any described taxon in corolla colour pattern,” the team wrote.

Industry observers note that the iNaturalist record came from Castelo de Alferce, in the municipality of Monchique. The plant clearly belonged to a group of toadflaxes called Linaria subsection Versicolores.

This observation prompted dedicated fieldwork in the Monchique Igneous Complex in 2024 and 2025.

In a recent development, on April 4, 2024, André Carapeto of the Portuguese Botanical Society collected the plant that became the holotype, the reference specimen for the species. He found it at an elevation of 1,027 feet (313 meters).

The holotype is kept in the herbarium of the University of Coimbra, with a duplicate at the Royal Botanical Garden in Madrid.

Sources indicate that the plant had been collected before without being recognized. Herbarium specimens gathered in 1995 and 1996 near Picota and in the Odelouca valley belong to the upcoming species.

The name honors the civil parish of Alferce, where the species was first recognized.

Sources indicate that the flower is deep yellow, with two orange to brownish-red stripes along the throat that split at the tip. The palate, the bulge that closes the mouth of the flower, is orange and often spotted with brownish red.

According to recent reports, flowers usually measure 0.8 to 0.9 inch (21 to 24 millimeters) long, including the spur. The erect flowering stems usually reach 6.7 to 15 inches (17 to 38 centimeters).

Recent findings suggest that the plant flowers and sets fruit from March to May. Its seeds are black to blackish gray and measure 0.02 to 0.03 inch (0.4 to 0.8 millimeter).

Its closest relatives are Linaria algarviana, which has violet-purple flowers, and Linaria bimaculata, whose throat stripes are rounded at the tip. Together, the three form a group of toadflaxes found only in the Algarve.

Its fruit capsules are longer than those of these two relatives, usually measuring 0.13 to 0.15 inch (3.4 to 3.8 millimeters).

It has been revealed that farminhão and Carapeto raised Linaria bimaculata to species rank in a 2024 study of Algarve toadflaxes, drawing on 78 iNaturalist records. Many of those records had first been uploaded under another species name.

It has been revealed that the Iberian branch of Linaria subsection Versicolores includes at least ten species. Toadflaxes belong to the tribe Antirrhineae of the plantain family, Plantaginaceae.

The new species grows mostly on soils derived from nepheline syenite, an igneous rock that makes up most of the Monchique Igneous Complex.

It occurs on the southern slopes of Serra da Picota, along the Odelouca river basin and near Marmelete. It favors annual meadows on gravel and sandy soils in clearings and on the edges of rocky heathland, often among boulders.

Industry observers note that the researchers combined DNA analysis, using a method called genotyping-by-sequencing, with a near-complete review of herbarium specimens. They also compared where these toadflaxes grow with geological maps.

According to recent reports, records from iNaturalist entered the analysis only if they were classified as reliable after a check of their photos. Most also had a location accurate to within about 490 feet (150 meters).

Sandstone, coarse sand, igneous rocks and windblown sand plains act as soil “islands” for these plants, while limestone, fine sands, shales and graywackes appear to work as barriers.

Together with shifts in flower color and shape, this pattern points to a role for geographic isolation and inferred soil specialization in the group’s diversification.

The authors propose a preliminary listing as Endangered under criterion B of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). The listing reflects the species’ small geographic range, declining habitat quality and few locations.

The species’ extent of occurrence covers about 34.6 square miles (89.6 square kilometers). It is known from four locations, and its area of occupancy is about 17 square miles (44 square kilometers).

Each locality holds fewer than 50 flowering plants, although the total population cannot be reliably estimated.

The main threat is believed to be the invasive silver wattle, Acacia dealbata, whose spread has intensified after recurrent wildfires. Native to southeastern Australia, it is legally listed as an invasive species in Portugal.

Recent findings suggest that the species has also lost habitat to eucalyptus plantations in the past. Forestry work, including road widening and timber storage, threatens plants along road verges, as does tourist development on the Picota slopes near Covão da Águia.

The study was published in the journal Plant Ecology and Evolution.

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

Sources indicate that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

According to recent reports, all that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

In a recent development, antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

Sources indicate that during that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off.".

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a major deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating.".

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an crucial question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

Industry observers note that the Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

#79. Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1229 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

Industry observers note that this capability could help advance technologies that are key to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

In a recent development, finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Industry observers note that mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

Sources indicate that "Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez remarked. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

The new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Latest Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

According to recent reports, light plays an key role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

Recent findings suggest that the newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

In a recent development, these differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez remarked.

Beyond identifying newly introduced candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for newly introduced medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

According to recent reports, the potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

"We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Sources indicate that martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

"At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

#78. Gut bacteria cannot see the sun so they use your meal times to control how your body absorbs nutrients

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words)
General 🌐 Earth

Gut bacteria cannot see the sun so they use your meal times to control how your body absorbs nutrients

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gut bacteria in mice read mealtimes, not daylight, and tell the intestine when to absorb, helping underfed mice grow and overfed ones get fat.
  • Recent findings suggest that the body clock is supposed to run on light.
  • In mice, a common microbe keeps time another way: it reads when food arrives and tells the cells of the intestine to start absorbing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gut bacteria in mice read mealtimes, not daylight, and tell the intestine when to absorb, helping underfed mice grow and overfed ones get fat.

Recent findings suggest that the body clock is supposed to run on light. Sunrise wakes the brain, and the rest of the body falls in line. But the bacteria in the gut live in the dark.

In mice, a common microbe keeps time another way: it reads when food arrives and tells the cells of the intestine to start absorbing.

Recent findings suggest that the signal is a small molecule the bacterium makes while it digests phytate, a compound in grains, nuts and seeds. The molecule switches on genes that pull amino acids and fats out of a meal.

Industry observers note that give it to undernourished young mice and they grow. Give it to mice on a high-fat diet and they get fatter.

It has been revealed that zheng Kuang, an associate professor of biological sciences at Carnegie Mellon University, led the work from his lab. Colleagues at the University of Pittsburgh, UT Southwestern Medical Center and the Quadram Institute in England took part.

All of it was done in mice and in human gut cells grown in a dish.

In an interview with Earth.com, Kuang said what struck him most was that the bacteria convert the timing of a meal into chemistry.

“Their absolute numbers did not need to change substantially across the day – their metabolic activity changed,” he remarked.

The bacterium is Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron, one of the most common residents of the human gut.

According to recent reports, kuang’s team raised mice with no gut microbes at all, then gave some of them this one species and nothing else. They sampled the lining of the small intestine around the clock.

According to recent reports, mice eat at night. In the hours after dark, the colonized mice carried more of the bacterial signal molecule in their gut lining than they did in the morning.

Germ-free mice revealed no such rise, and neither did mice given a mutant strain missing the enzyme that breaks down phytate.

The bacteria themselves were no more numerous at night than in the morning, Kuang’s team found. What rose was the activity of that one enzyme.

Industry observers note that “We are not claiming these bacteria have their own internal clock,” Kuang told Earth.com. “Rather, they respond to feeding cues and produce molecules called inositol phosphates, which activate a protein called HDAC3 in intestinal cells.”.

That protein, HDAC3, works inside the cells lining the intestine and helps decide which genes are on.

The bacterial molecule makes it grip a partner protein more tightly, and the pair then turns on a set of transporter genes that carry nutrients across the gut wall.

In colonized mice, 14 amino acids and 14 fatty acids rose in the blood during the feeding hours, while in germ-free mice they stayed low.

Of 248 transporter genes the team tracked, 122 cycled more strongly with the bacterium present, and most of those handle amino acids, sugars or fats.

According to recent reports, the body’s master clock genes kept their normal daily rhythm either way. The bacterium didn’t reset the clock; it strengthened the daily rise and fall of the metabolic genes that follow it.

According to recent reports, the team then fed mice only during the day, which is their normal sleeping time. The signal molecule fell and the gut’s daily rhythm in gene activity flattened, though the animals ate no less than before.

Mice allowed to eat only at night looked like mice allowed to eat whenever they liked.

Sources indicate that the feeding experiment is the result Kuang pointed to when asked what people should take from the work. “The key message is to align your feeding schedule with the natural day-night cycle – eating during your active, daytime hours,” he noted.

Artificial light has pushed human eating into the night, he added, and the study suggests that misalignment disrupts the bacterial signals.

Recent findings suggest that kuang noted there was likely a metabolic cost to that disruption. The feeding experiment itself tracked the signal and the gene rhythms, not the mice’s weight.

Young mice were weaned onto a diet with the usual calories but little protein or fat, a model for childhood malnutrition.

Those given the bacterium grew longer bodies and longer thigh bones than those given the mutant strain. They had heavier organs, more amino acids in their blood and better blood sugar control, and they ate the same amount.

It has been revealed that the signal molecule on its own did the same, in mice with and without a normal gut community. In mice bred to lack HDAC3 in their gut cells, neither the bacterium nor the molecule helped, and a drug that blocks HDAC3 blunted the effect too.

In a public dataset of children’s stool samples, the bacterium was among 19 species more common in healthy children than in undernourished ones.

Adult mice fed a high-fat, high-sugar diet for 12 weeks gained more weight with the bacterium than with the mutant strain.

Industry observers note that they carried more belly fat and liver fat and had higher blood fats and worse blood sugar handling. They absorbed more fat from food and passed less of it in their stool.

Again, the mice lacking HDAC3 in their gut cells showed none of this, and food intake didn’t differ.

Kuang remarked that double edge is the finding he most wants understood. “This illustrates why it is too simple to label a bacterium as inherently ‘good’ or ‘bad’ – its effects depend on diet and the metabolic state of the host,” he explained.

The team’s reading is evolutionary. A pathway that extracts the most from every meal was an advantage when food was scarce, and the same pathway can work against a body surrounded by high-fat diets.

In a recent development, whether this bacterium even lives and works in the human small intestine is an open question. The team also could not prove that the signal molecule in the gut cells came from the bacteria rather than from the cells themselves, which make related molecules.

And phytate intake varies from one diet to another, so the signal’s strength probably does too, the authors wrote.

Whether the same signal shifts in people who eat on a jet-lagged or night-shift schedule is a question the study does not reach.

Asked how soon the bacteria could be tested against malnutrition, Kuang said it is too early to give a reliable timeline for human testing.

Industry observers note that the next step, he mentioned, is to look for the pathway in human intestinal samples and in children with undernutrition. Until then, the case that mealtimes talk to the gut through its bacteria rests on mice.

The full study was published online in a publication of the Carnegie Mellon University.

#77. Industry News: Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

Industry News: Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read | Source: Sciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every print subscription comes with full digital access.
  • By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover.

Every print subscription comes with full digital access.

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover.

In a recent development, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani claims gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he claims. “That is the best kind of discovery.”.

#76. Latest Update: Why do we feel colder as we age? Scientists are tracing the signals

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words)
General 🌐 Earth

Latest Update: Why do we feel colder as we age? Scientists are tracing the signals

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mouse study suggests immune signals slow brown fat’s response to cold with age, offering clues to why older bodies struggle to stay warm.
  • Industry observers note that an older person can feel chilly in a room that feels comfortable to someone younger.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a upcoming mouse study, this fat took much longer to respond to cold in old animals than in young ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mouse study suggests immune signals slow brown fat’s response to cold with age, offering clues to why older bodies struggle to stay warm.

Industry observers note that an older person can feel chilly in a room that feels comfortable to someone younger. Some of the explanation may lie in brown fat, which burns sugar and fat to supply the body with heat.

Recent findings suggest that in a upcoming mouse study, this fat took much longer to respond to cold in old animals than in young ones. The researchers followed that difference back to a substance released by nearby immune cells.

Older brown fat had more of this substance, which helps hold down heat production. A separate drug experiment demonstrated that the mice could recover some of their lost warmth.

Recent findings suggest that anying Song and Qiong A. Wang led the work. Wang, an associate professor at City of Hope, is a corresponding author.

In young mice at room temperature, 28.8% of brown fat cells were in a state that produces lots of heat. The share more than doubled to 61.7% after a day in the cold, reaching 89.7% by the third day.

Recent findings suggest that mice aged about 74 weeks started far lower, at 0.31%. Three days later, the figure was 50.9%, still short of the younger animals’ level on day one.

Sources indicate that the older mice got colder while their fat was making this slow adjustment. Within two days, 25% had died.

It has been revealed that the laboratory’s 2020 work had shown that the cells differed in their supply of a protein called UCP1. A brown fat cell uses this protein to make heat.

There was plenty of UCP1 in some cells and hardly any in others. Those with little of it were doing less of the heating.

In a recent development, in these less active cells, another protein called H6PD was more abundant. H6PD helps the cells maintain a supply of active stress hormone.

Cortisol is the main stress hormone in humans, while corticosterone plays that role in mice.

With this hormone acting inside them, the fat cells respond less strongly to nerve signals that call for more heat.

Recent findings suggest that at 75°F (24°C), the mouse tissue contained about as many cells in one group as in the other. Only a few cells had both proteins.

For the human part of the study, the researchers used tissue from five patients who had thyroid surgery in Ancona, Italy.

Colleagues at Marche Polytechnic University helped examine the fat, which came from above the collarbone.

The human cells divided into two nearly equal groups as well. These patients were between 18 and 48 years old, leaving the researchers without samples from older adults.

The young mice spent a week in a room at 43°F (6°C). By the end, the cells making plenty of heat accounted for 85.6%, up from 31.1% before their stay in the cold.

Once the animals were warm again, the change went into reverse.

To check the part played by nerves, the team cut their connection to brown fat on one side of young mice. In cold conditions, 85.6% of cells on the side with working nerves became highly active, compared with 29.1% on the side without them.

That second side looked pale, too, as brown fat does when it makes little heat. It was in the same cold surroundings as the other side, but couldn’t receive the nerve messages.

The nerves release noradrenaline, so the researchers tried adding that chemical to fat cells in a dish. H6PD levels stayed as they were.

Industry observers note that the next clue involved two types of immune cells found in the fat, neutrophils and macrophages. Some of them made IL-1 beta, a substance involved in inflammation.

According to recent reports, after a week in the cold, the team measured 53% less IL-1 beta in brown fat. Moving mice into a warm room raised its level 3.3-fold.

In a recent development, IL-1 beta was produced by 10% of neutrophils and 1% of macrophages in the tissue. Under the microscope, less active fat cells lay closer to these immune cells, while cells making more heat lay farther away.

It has been revealed that this arrangement suggested that the immune cells could have an effect on their nearest neighbors. The team also worked out how IL-1 beta kept those fat cells from making much heat.

According to recent reports, it kept H6PD from breaking down, so the amount of this protein rose 3.5-fold. With its supply maintained, the active stress hormone could keep heat production low.

When the researchers blocked IL-1 beta inside brown fat, the balance of more active cells to less active ones doubled at room temperature. Blood levels of the signal didn’t change along with it.

Older brown fat contained six times as much IL-1 beta and 1.8 times as much active stress hormone, although blood hormone levels weren’t higher.

It also had 2.3 times as much of the protein supporting that hormone and 40% less of the protein used to make heat.

Recent findings suggest that extra weight didn’t produce the same pattern. All the young mice that became obese on a high-fat diet survived a week in the cold, and their brown fat appeared more active.

The researchers tried mifepristone, a drug that blocks the receptor through which the stress hormone acts. They gave it to 72-week-old mice for a week.

In a recent development, without treatment, only 0.5% of cells were in the active group at room temperature; with the drug, 8.3% were. After a cold day, those figures were 10.6% and 32.8%.

The treated animals stayed warmer, and their brown fat contained smaller fat droplets. They burned more energy and used more oxygen through day and night, although they neither ate more nor moved more.

Removing the hormone receptor from active fat cells in another experiment also kept heat production going.

It continued for days after the mice returned to warmth, using extra fuel even though the animals’ food intake hadn’t changed.

Recent findings suggest that mifepristone isn’t a treatment for feeling cold. Because it acts in many tissues, the experiment couldn’t pin all the improvements on brown fat.

All the mice were male, and the human samples included no older adults.

“Learning how the body controls this process may offer insights into obesity, type 2 diabetes and other metabolic disorders,” said Wang.

“That possibility matters for more than staying warm. Thermogenic fat also burns glucose and fat, and its activity tends to decline with age.”.

For the older mice, at least, some capacity to make heat remained. The experiments revealed that changing the signals reaching their fat cells could bring some of it back.

The study is published in the journal Nature.

60 years ago, the Leonid meteor shower unleashed one of the most spectacular meteor storms in recorded history. As the 2026 peak approaches, here's what skywatchers can expect.

Industry observers note that when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

According to recent reports, this year marks a rather auspicious anniversary for meteor watchers. Sixty years ago, one of the most stupendous Leonid meteor displays lit up the predawn skies over the central and western U.S. So, what will the 2026 Leonids bring us? And what might they bring in the years to come?

The Leonid meteor shower is one of the most celebrated of the year's annual displays of "shooting stars." The mere mention of the Leonids usually elicits mental images of a sky filled with shooting stars pouring down through the sky like rain. Such meteor storms have indeed occurred with the Leonids, such as in 1833 and 1966 when meteor rates of tens of thousands per hour were observed. In more recent years, most notably 1999, 2001 and 2002, lesser Leonid displays of up to "only" a few thousand meteors per hour took place.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, that's not likely to be the case this year. In fact, comparatively speaking, this is going to be a lean year for the Leonids chiefly because of the expected lack of any significant activity. Although the Leonids are one of the most famous of all the annual meteor displays, this year they're not likely to be very productive. It's probable they are going to be rather weak and there probably will be long stretches when not a single Leonid will be seen. I'll explain why in a moment. First, let's find out about this shower's lineage.

Industry observers note that the Leonids are so named because the shower's radiant point, from where the meteors seem to fan out, is located within the constellation of Leo the Lion, from the backward question mark pattern of stars known as "The Sickle." The meteors are caused by the Tempel-Tuttle comet, which sweeps through the inner solar system every 33⅓ years. Each time the comet passes closest to the sun it leaves a "river of rubble" in its wake: a dense trail of dusty debris. A meteor storm becomes possible if the Earth were to score a direct hit on a fresh dust trail ejected by the comet over the past several centuries.

Recent findings suggest that the "lion's share" (no pun intended) of comet dust can be found just ahead and trailing behind Tempel-Tuttle. That comet last swept through the inner solar system in 1998. That's why spectacular meteor showers were seen in 1999, 2001 and 2002, with declining numbers thereafter.

According to the International Meteor Organization's 2026 meteor shower calendar, the Leonids are expected to reach their regular maximum at 23:45 UTC (6:45 p.m. EST) on Nov. 17, with around 15 meteors per hour possible under ideal viewing conditions.

Other forecasts place the peak at slightly different times. Margaret Campbell-Brown and Peter Brown, meteor experts for the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada, predict that the peak of this year's Leonids will occur at 00:00 hours UTC on Nov. 18. Russian meteor expert Mikhail Maslov feels that the peak will come about a third of a day earlier, at 16:00 UTC on Nov. 17.

Sources indicate that several weaker encounters with older debris trails are also predicted between Nov. 17 and 19, although no major meteor storm is expected.

Back in September 2014, comet Tempel-Tuttle was as far from the sun as it can get: 1.84 billion miles (2.96 billion km). The comet has since spent the last dozen years slowly approaching the inner solar system, but it's still 1.11 billion miles (1.79 billion km) from the sun, which is still well beyond the orbit of Saturn.

In contrast, at the point in the comet's orbit where we will be passing by on Tuesday morning, there is nothing save for a scattered few particles; bits and pieces likely loosened from the comet's nucleus a millennium or two ago.

So, this year's Leonids are expected to show only low activity; "maybe" at best 10 to 15 Leonids per hour might be seen, but more likely hourly counts will be less than that. The moon will not pose a problem; it's at first quarter phase, but it will set before 11 p.m. local time Monday evening, leaving the rest of the night dark.

Watching a meteor shower consists of lying back, looking up at the sky... and waiting. Keep in mind that any local light pollution or obstructions like tall trees or buildings will further reduce your chances of making a meteor sighting. Leo does not start coming fully into view until the after-midnight hours, so that would be the best time to concentrate on looking for Leonids. As dawn is about to break at around 5 a.m., the Sickle will have climbed more than two-thirds of the way up from the southeast horizon to the point directly overhead (called the zenith).

In a recent development, because the Leonids are moving along in their orbit around the sun in a direction opposite to that of Earth, they slam into our atmosphere nearly head-on, resulting in the fastest meteor velocities possible: 45 miles (72 km) per second. Such speeds tend to produce bright meteors, which leave long-lasting streaks or persistent trains in their wake. A mighty Leonid fireball can be quite spectacular, but such outstandingly bright meteors are likely to be very few and very far between this year (if any are seen at all).

It was a different story 60 years ago, in 1966, when anticipation ran high for a potentially heavy display of Leonid meteors. The previous year, comet Tempel-Tuttle swept around the sun and was accompanied later that year by an unexpected surge of Leonid activity, with brilliant meteors darting across the sky at one or two per minute as seen from Hawaii and Australia. The most sanguine prediction for 1966 came from Dr. Kenneth L. Franklin (1923-2007), chief scientist at Fresh York's Hayden Planetarium. Dr. Franklin had carefully examined the orbit of comet Tempel-Tuttle and concluded that " . . . the position of the comet is roughly what it was in 1833. So, a dramatic shower like the one that occurred in that year may yet be in the offing for 1966.".

In a recent development, based on Dr. Franklin's prediction, a "meteor party" was planned for the peak night of the Leonids in Central Park. Latest Yorkers of all ages were invited to gather on the Great Lawn at midnight to watch for the shooting stars. Ten thousand people turned out, but unfortunately skies were hopelessly cloudy.

Sources indicate that but across the central and western US, where skies were mostly clear, Leonids were falling at a rate described by many as "too numerous to count." One observer stationed north of Mission, Texas noted that meteors falling in all directions gave the impression of a "gigantic umbrella," appearing to "waterfall" out of the head of Leo. Perhaps the best views were from California and Arizona. At the Table Mountain Observatory, near Wrightwood, California, one resident astronomer commented that he and a colleague " . . . watched a rain of meteors, turn into a hail of meteors and finally a storm of meteors, too numerous to count by 3:50 a.m. Pacific Time. Instinctively we sought to shield our upturned faces from imagined celestial debris." From 6,850-foot Kitt Peak in southern Arizona, thirteen amateur astronomers saw Leonids falling at the staggering rate of 40 per second (144,000 per hour)!

It has been revealed that in 2005, French meteor expert Jeremie Vaubaillon published a technical paper with two colleagues in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics that forecast Leonid activity for years up to 2100. Sadly, in the year 2029, Jupiter is expected to throw Comet Tempel-Tuttle off its current path through space, making it all but impossible — at least through the beginning of the 22nd century — to see a repeat of the Great Leonid Storm of 1966. But Vaubaillon expects the next significant Leonid outburst in the year 2034, when rates could reach up to 2,000 per hour.

Sources indicate that that's just 8 years from now. Mark your calendars.

Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at Latest York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky and Telescope, The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

Joe Rao is Space.com's skywatching columnist, as well as a veteran meteorologist and eclipse chaser who also serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky & Telescope and other publications. Joe is an 8-time Emmy-nominated meteorologist who served the Putnam Valley region of New York for over 21 years. You can find him on Twitter and YouTube tracking lunar and solar eclipses, meteor showers and more. To find out Joe's latest project, visit him on Twitter.

#73. Tech Report: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8 min read (1683 words)
Business & Policy 🌐 Sciencedaily

Tech Report: Dark energy may have flipped from negative to positive 9.5 billion years ago

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, scientists have generally assumed that dark energy, the mysterious component thought to be responsible for the Universe's accelerating expansion, has remained constant throughout cosmic history.
  • Industry observers note that researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) have explored that possibility by taking a fresh look at an established alternative theory of gravity.
  • Sources indicate that the research was conducted within Akarsu's group at ITU, alongside postdoctoral researcher Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, scientists have generally assumed that dark energy, the mysterious component thought to be responsible for the Universe's accelerating expansion, has remained constant throughout cosmic history. That long-standing assumption is now facing new scrutiny. Observations from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), which is constructing the largest three-dimensional map of the Universe, suggest that dark energy's influence may have changed over billions of years. Although the evidence is not yet strong enough to establish a discovery, it has renewed interest in a fundamental question: Could dark energy evolve rather than remain constant?

Industry observers note that researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) have explored that possibility by taking a fresh look at an established alternative theory of gravity. In a 2025 study published in Physical Review D, an international team led by Prof. Özgür Akarsu of ITU's Department of Physics investigated a mathematical possibility that previous researchers had largely overlooked. Their analysis revealed a surprising scenario in which the effective density of dark energy was negative during the Universe's early history before eventually becoming positive.

Sources indicate that the research was conducted within Akarsu's group at ITU, alongside postdoctoral researcher Dr. N. Merve Uzun and doctoral student Bilal Bulduk. The team also collaborated with Prof. Nihan Katırcı of Doğuş University, who previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in Akarsu's group, and Prof. Antonio De Felice of Kyoto University's Yukawa Institute for Theoretical Physics, an internationally recognized center for theoretical physics.

An Overlooked Possibility in Einstein's Theory of Gravity.

The discovery came from examining a part of an existing theory that had received relatively little attention. Rather than proposing an entirely latest explanation for dark energy, the researchers revisited a framework known as teleparallel f(T) gravity.

Industry observers note that einstein's general theory of relativity explains gravity through the curvature of spacetime. Teleparallel gravity takes a different mathematical approach, describing gravity through a property called torsion. Scientists have spent years studying modified versions of this framework to investigate whether gravity itself might account for the Universe's accelerating expansion.

It has been revealed that earlier investigations of an exponential form of teleparallel gravity had concentrated on one particular set of mathematical solutions. This approach reflected a familiar assumption inherited from general relativity: dark energy should always have a positive density.

In a recent development, akarsu and his colleagues decided to investigate what would happen if that restriction were removed. By considering a previously neglected branch of the theory, they uncovered a substantially different picture of how the Universe might have evolved.

Dark Energy May Have Switched From Negative to Positive.

The team's calculations showed that two distinct cosmic histories could emerge even when the Universe contains the same amount of matter today.

According to recent reports, one mathematical solution closely resembles the standard model of cosmology. The other predicts that effective dark energy had a negative density in the distant past. According to this second possibility, the density reached zero at approximately redshift 1.5, corresponding to roughly 9.5 billion years ago, before becoming positive and remaining that way.

What makes the result particularly interesting is that the researchers did not need to introduce an additional adjustable parameter to produce this behavior. Instead, the determining factor is related to the Universe's present matter density, which selects the mathematical branch. As a result, the model retains the same six cosmological parameters used in the standard ΛCDM model.

It has been revealed that the theory also avoids an vital potential problem. Although it predicts behavior that differs from Einstein's gravity across enormous cosmic distances, its departures from general relativity become naturally suppressed in dense environments. This allows the alternative solution to remain compatible with the highly accurate measurements of gravity made throughout the Solar System.

A Possible Explanation for the Hubble Tension.

The latest findings build on years of research into whether dark energy could have changed sign during the Universe's history.

Sources indicate that akarsu and his collaborators previously developed a framework called the sign-switching ΛCDM (ΛsCDM) model. In this scenario, the cosmological constant changes from negative to positive several billion years after the Substantial Bang.

It has been revealed that previous analyses found that a change in the sign of dark energy's density could agree with DESI observations while potentially reducing several unresolved disagreements in cosmology. One of the most significant is the Hubble tension, the persistent discrepancy between different methods of measuring the Universe's present expansion rate.

In a recent development, however, an important question remained unanswered. What underlying physical process could cause dark energy to undergo such a reversal?

In a recent development, the latest research offers a possible mechanism. Instead of requiring scientists to prescribe a sign change as part of the model, the reversal arises naturally from the mathematical structure of the modified gravity theory.

Akarsu explained why investigating an overlooked solution proved so valuable.

"For several years we have been studying a scenario in which dark energy switches sign, and it has held up remarkably well against data such as DESI's. The open question was what physical mechanism could produce such behavior. So we deliberately looked at a branch of a well-known theory of gravity that had been set aside because it violates the usual expectation that the dark energy density stays positive. The sign change emerged naturally from the theory itself.".

DESI Observations Raise Newly introduced Questions About Dark Energy.

The theoretical findings have become especially relevant as astronomers gather increasingly detailed measurements of cosmic expansion.

Sources indicate that DESI tracks the locations of millions of galaxies and quasars, allowing researchers to reconstruct how the Universe has expanded across billions of years. In March 2025, the DESI collaboration released findings based on its first three years of observations.

When combined with measurements of the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and weak gravitational lensing, the results strengthened earlier indications that dark energy might not behave like a fixed cosmological constant.

In a recent development, these findings do not yet establish that dark energy changes over time. The statistical significance depends on which observational datasets are combined, and the evidence remains below the threshold required to claim a definitive discovery. Nevertheless, the possibility has motivated scientists to investigate alternative descriptions of cosmic expansion.

According to recent reports, DESI has now completed its planned five-year survey, observing more than 47 million galaxies and quasars. The complete dataset will provide an even more demanding test of whether the apparent changes in dark energy persist as measurements become more precise.

In a recent development, the timing is also noteworthy. The ITU-led team's research was initially submitted in October 2024, several months before DESI confirmed its March 2025 findings. The researchers have not yet tested their model against the complete DESI dataset, making that comparison an notable next step.

Could the Universe's Accelerating Expansion Be Slowing?

The significance of the proposed model extends beyond its prediction that dark energy's density may have changed sign.

Sources indicate that because the alternative solution emerges from a specific theory of gravity, it makes predictions about both cosmic expansion and how gravity behaves across the Universe. These predictions give astronomers ways to investigate whether the proposed cosmic history is consistent with observations.

Industry observers note that measurements of how galaxies and larger structures form and grow will be particularly important. Researchers can also examine how gravity bends light and how the Universe's expansion has changed over time. Among the most useful observational tests are structure growth, redshift-space distortions, and weak gravitational lensing.

Although comprehensive testing remains necessary, the initial results offer reasons for further investigation.

In an extended version of the theory that includes a cosmological constant, the researchers found that the model could remain consistent with observations of the cosmic microwave background while allowing the higher present-day expansion rates obtained from local measurements. This makes it a potentially useful approach to understanding the Hubble tension.

Sources indicate that the extended model also permits another intriguing possibility: the acceleration of the Universe's expansion could have weakened or even stopped in the relatively recent cosmic past. Recent studies examining DESI observations have raised similar questions about whether cosmic acceleration has remained steady.

Importantly, neither the proposed dark energy reversal nor a recent slowdown in cosmic acceleration has been established as an observational fact. Both remain possibilities that must be tested against increasingly precise data.

Revisiting Gravity Could Reveal a Different Cosmic History.

The research highlights how familiar scientific theories can contain possibilities that were missed because earlier investigations relied on restrictive assumptions.

In this case, allowing effective dark energy to have a negative density exposed an alternative evolutionary history within an already established mathematical framework. The researchers suggest that examining similarly overlooked solutions in other modified gravity theories could lead to additional insights.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the strength of the fresh explanation will depend on how well it reproduces the Universe astronomers actually observe. The full DESI dataset and other cosmological measurements will help determine whether this unusual version of cosmic history deserves a place alongside established explanations.

"We identified an alternative path for the Universe within an existing theory. The next step is to test it rigorously against the full observational data. The preliminary picture is encouraging, and we are particularly interested in what it may tell us about the Hubble tension," said Prof. Özgür Akarsu.
