#48. The Sky This Week from November 13 to 20: The Leonids peak

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11 min read (2222 words)
General 🌐 Astronomy

The Sky This Week from November 13 to 20: The Leonids peak

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read | Source: Astronomy

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Friday, November 20The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M.
  • According to recent reports, already 60° high in the east by 8 P.M.
  • It has been revealed that any telescope will show M33, but larger ones are better because its considerable size — some 70’ across along its longer axis — spreads its light out and makes its surface brightness quite low.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Friday, November 20The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth.

According to recent reports, already 60° high in the east by 8 P.M. local time is M33, the Pinwheel Galaxy in Triangulum. This lovely spiral glows at 6th magnitude and is technically visible from a dark site with sharp eyes — just wait until after moonset if you want to give it a try. You’ll find it in far western Triangulum, about 4.3° west-northwest of 3rd-magnitude Alpha (α) Trianguli.

It has been revealed that any telescope will show M33, but larger ones are better because its considerable size — some 70’ across along its longer axis — spreads its light out and makes its surface brightness quite low. Instruments 10 inches or larger will show some detail along the spiral arms, including brighter knots of star formation.

Located some 2.7 million light-years away, M33 is the third-largest galaxy in our Local Group, after Andromeda and our own Milky Way. This cosmic neighbor is a classic spiral with no central bar and a round, bright nucleus wrapped by its dusty arms. Oriented more closely to face-on than Andromeda, M33 is a popular target for visual observers as well as astrophotographers.

Sunrise: 6:43 A.M. Sunset: 4:45 P.M. Moonrise: 10:54 A.M. Moonset: 7:55 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (21%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Saturday, November 14Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.

Sources indicate that this morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.

Recent findings suggest that both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.

Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:44 A.M. Sunset: 4:44 P.M. Moonrise: 11:33 A.M. Moonset: 8:56 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%).

Recent findings suggest that sunday, November 15Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

Sunrise: 6:45 A.M. Sunset: 4:43 P.M. Moonrise: 12:05 P.M. Moonset: 9:58 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (38%).

Sources indicate that monday, November 16It’s a great night to catch Saturn’s largest and brightest moon, Titan, as it skims south of the planet. Two hours after sunset, Saturn is roughly 40° high in the southeast, outshining all the other stars in this region of the sky. It lies to the lower left of the Circlet of Pisces and to the upper left of the bright star Fomalhaut in Piscis Austrinus.

Zoom in on Saturn with a telescope to first catch sight of its ring system, stretching 43” from end to end and tilted 8° to our line of sight. Currently we are seeing Saturn’s southern side, including the entirety of the planet’s southern hemisphere. The gas giant’s disk now measures 19” across.

According to recent reports, titan is difficult to miss, shining at mid-8th magnitude just south of the ringed planet. Don’t be fooled by a fainter 10th-magnitude field star, which lies just to Titan’s west. The three next-brightest moons, also 10th magnitude, are Tethys, Dione, and Rhea. They lie closer to the planet. Tethys sits about 40” west of Saturn’s center shortly before 8 P.M. EST, while Dione is just west of the limb and Rhea just east of the planet. Dione and Rhea are moving westward, and Rhea will skim just north of Saturn’s pole along the way, standing due north of the planet around 10:40 P.M. EST. Tethys is moving east, and will disappear behind the planet’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 2:35 A.M. EST on the 16th (still late on the 15th along the Pacific Coast).

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:46 A.M. Sunset: 4:43 P.M. Moonrise: 12:32 P.M. Moonset: 11:00 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (47%).

In a recent development, tuesday, November 17First Quarter Moon occurs at 6:48 A.M. EST, floating among the stars of Aquarius.

It has been revealed that early this evening brighter targets are best, as the Moon doesn’t set until late. Ready for viewing as the winter constellations start to dominate earlier each day is the Pleiades, an open cluster cataloged as M45.

It has been revealed that known since antiquity and readily visible to the naked eye, the Pleiades contains several bright stars arranged in a tiny dipperlike shape. Located in northwestern Taurus, the cluster is sometimes mistaken for the Little Dipper, although that asterism is much larger and lies in the northern sky, anchored at the end of its handle by Polaris, the North Star. The Pleiades shines with a collective magnitude of 1.6 and spans roughly 110’ — a huge swath of sky. It lies above the sideways V-shape of Taurus’ face as the Bull rises in the east this evening, and is already 30° high by 7:30 P.M. local time. How many stars can you make out with the naked eye? Most observers see six or seven.

Recent findings suggest that once you’ve taken in the cluster without any optical aid, zoom in with binoculars or a finder scope. (Any higher magnification and you won’t see most of the cluster at once, but instead be limited to a smaller portion.) Many more stars will now pop into your field of view. If you do opt for high magnification, look for a faint grayish haze around the stars — this is nearby dust reflecting the stars’ light, and requires clear, dark conditions to make out.

Sources indicate that the Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight, with the best meteor viewing overnight into the early-morning hours of November 18, as the Moon sets around midnight and the radiant rises higher. Check out tomorrow’s entry for more detail.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:47 A.M. Sunset: 4:42 P.M. Moonrise: 12:56 P.M. Moonset: — Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (57%).

Wednesday, November 18The peak of the Leonid meteor shower, caused by the dusty debris of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, is best seen early this morning after the Moon has set and the shower’s radiant rises high in the hours before dawn.

Two hours before sunrise, Leo is high in the southeast, with bright Jupiter and Mars joining the curved shape of the Sickle asterism. The Leonids’ radiant is located just inside the cuved blade’s inner edge, near 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Leonis to the upper left (north) of Mars and Jupiter. The two planets appear roughly side by side in the sky around this time, with ruddy Mars at left and more golden-yellow Jupiter at right. Regulus sits just to their lower left.

To catch the most meteors, you’ll actually want to look a little ways away from Leo, about 40° to 60° to the left or right of the constellation. This is where meteors with the longest trains will also occur. Although this shower isn’t particularly strong, you can expect to see roughly a half-dozen or more Leonid meteors per hour. The Leonid shower produces some of the fastest-moving meteors we experience all year, streaking through the sky at some 44 miles (70 kilometers) per hour.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 6:49 A.M. Sunset: 4:41 P.M. Moonrise: 1:19 P.M. Moonset: 12:03 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (67%).

In a recent development, thursday, November 19The solar system is a dynamic place. Let’s return to the predawn sky today to check out the inner planets’ progress relative to the stars of Virgo. An hour before sunrise, both Mercury and Venus are again well above the eastern horizon, with the stars around them still visible before twilight brightens too much.

Industry observers note that compared with earlier in the week, Venus now sits to the upper left of Spica, rather than directly above it. Venus will pass 1.8° due north of Spica later today at 6 P.M. EST. Now moving steadily east, it will track along the ecliptic, slowly headed for Libra. Mercury has already reached the Balance, sitting within its domain and to the far lower left of Kappa (κ) Virginis, as opposed to the pair’s close proximity a few days ago.

It has been revealed that pull out your telescope to see how the planets’ appearances have changed, too. Mercury is now 55% lit and 7” across, while Venus is 18% lit and has shrunk more noticeably, now 47” across.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise: 6:50 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 1:41 P.M. Moonset: 1:07 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (76%).

Friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST; 12 hours later, our satellite passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. The trio is visible in the southeastern sky two hours after sunset, forming a triangle with the Moon to the upper left of Saturn, and Neptune to Saturn’s right. Only the Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, while Neptune will require optical aid.

Recent findings suggest that from the gibbous Moon, drop down first to check out Saturn through a telescope, including its lovely ring system and brightest moon, Titan. Saturn is the brightest object in this part of the sky after the Moon, so you don’t have to worry about misidentifying it. After passing south of the ringed world earlier this week, Titan now sits about 3.2’ to Saturn’s west, in line with the rings. Fainter moons Tethys, Rhea, and Dione may be visible clustered closer to the planet, but the bright moonlight might also make them challenging for visual observation.

Industry observers note that from Saturn, scan 6.6° west-southwest to land on Neptune. If you have a go-to scope, it may take you right to the outermost planet, which glows at magnitude 7.7 and offers up a tiny, 2”-wide disk. It may look like a “flat,” bluish-gray star, rather than a bright pinprick of white light. Look for a large parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars just over 9° to Saturn’s southwest if you need a closer stepping stone. The star at the northeastern point of that shape is 5th-magnitude 29 Piscium, and it lies about 2.6° southwest of Neptune.

Mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST. We’ll check out the planet in the predawn sky in next week’s column.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%).

#47. Did El Niño cause an early breakdown in the polar vortex?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (747 words)
General 🌐 Newscientist

Did El Niño cause an early breakdown in the polar vortex?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Newscientist

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Check your subscription status, enhancement your details and more.
  • The polar vortex has suffered an unprecedented early breakdown, threatening Europe with cold and snow, and some scientists think the record super El Niño is to blame.
  • The polar vortex, a high-altitude band of westerly winds circling the Arctic that bottles up cold air over the north pole, typically strengthens through the winter and weakens in the spring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Check your subscription status, enhancement your details and more.

The polar vortex has suffered an unprecedented early breakdown, threatening Europe with cold and snow, and some scientists think the record super El Niño is to blame.

The polar vortex, a high-altitude band of westerly winds circling the Arctic that bottles up cold air over the north pole, typically strengthens through the winter and weakens in the spring.

Is a broken jet stream causing extreme weather that lasts longer?

The El Niño climate phase, which has already warmed surface waters in the tropical Pacific to record temperatures and continues to heat up, tends to keep the vortex strong in autumn and early winter. Then, in late winter, it often weakens the vortex, allowing that cold air to spill southwards into Europe and sometimes North America.

According to recent reports, but on 10 November, the polar vortex weakened to the point that it broke down, with the winds reversing direction to blow weakly from the east. While these collapses happen every few years, they almost never occur in November. This is the earliest it has happened since weather balloon records began in the 1950s, beating the old record by 18 days.

This may have been due to random fluctuations in the atmosphere. It is also possible, however, that the extremely strong El Niño could have sped up the weakening of the polar vortex that typically happens later in the winter, though that isn’t proven, according to Adam Scaife at the Met Office, the UK’s weather service.

Recent findings suggest that “There probably is some kind of El Niño influence on it,” he states. “That would be my suspicion, but we don’t know that for sure.”.

In a recent development, as east-to-west trade winds weaken during El Niño and the warm water they built up in the western Pacific washes back eastwards, a low-pressure centre of warm, rising air moves eastwards with it. This causes extra waviness in the jet stream, another band of strong westerly winds that circles the globe, except further south and lower in the atmosphere than the polar vortex. The jet stream meanders further southwards around Alaska, deepening a low-pressure system there called the Aleutian low.

But the El Niño-linked wave doesn’t just propagate side to side in the jet stream. It can also propagate upwards into the stratosphere, where the polar vortex is. As the air gets thinner, the wave’s amplitude gets bigger until it crashes into the polar vortex like a wave crashing onto a beach, claims Scaife. And while the polar vortex is westerly, these waves carry easterly momentum.

“When they dump that momentum, they push the polar vortex against its flow, and they weaken it,” he notes.

5 graphs that show how the record-breaking El Niño will affect the world.

But another reason for the polar vortex breakdown could be a high-pressure “blocking” system that developed over Scandinavia in recent weeks, which blocked the jet stream and caused large meanders in it. This waviness could also have weakened the polar vortex through the same wave-breaking process, regardless of El Niño.

In a recent development, “I would be wary of saying it was caused by El Niño,” says Andrew Charlton-Perez at the University of Reading, UK. “I would say the blocking high is probably more crucial.”.

The reversal of the polar vortex isn’t related to the current cold weather in the UK. But it could bring even more cold, snowy weather in the coming weeks.

It has been revealed that A polar vortex breakdown is also known as a sudden stratospheric warming event. As the winds weaken, high-level air rushes in over the north pole, increasing atmospheric pressure and raising temperatures, just as pumping up a bike tyre warms it up.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, over the following weeks, cold surface-level air can descend from the Arctic into northern Europe. A polar vortex breakdown preceded the “Beast from the East” cold snap in 2018, when blizzards covered much of the UK in snow and killed 10 people.

While the polar vortex is expected to strengthen towards the end of November, bringing warmer weather, it could break down again this winter, Scaife warns.

“The risk of cold easterlies this winter is increasing,” he claims.

Latest Update: Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread.
  • Industry observers note that the findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying.
  • Sources indicate that "Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," mentioned Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers at The Wistar Institute have discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy can release fructose, which acts as a signal that encourages nearby tumor cells to break free and spread.

Industry observers note that the findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying. The discovery also raises notable questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses.

Sources indicate that "Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," mentioned Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study. "Instead, they continue to release molecules that send signals to nearby cells. Our study is among the first to show that a nutrient -- in this case, fructose -- can act as one of those signals.".

Why Ovarian Cancer Often Returns After Chemotherapy.

Most patients with ovarian cancer receive platinum-based chemotherapy, a treatment that uses drugs containing platinum to damage the DNA of cancer cells and prevent them from reproducing. Although many patients initially respond well, the cancer eventually returns in most cases. It also frequently spreads throughout the abdominal cavity, the space inside the abdomen that contains organs such as the stomach, intestines, and liver.

This spread, known as metastasis, is responsible for approximately 90% of ovarian cancer deaths. Understanding what allows cancer cells to escape from their original location and establish new tumors is therefore a major priority for researchers.

Previous studies have suggested that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy may contribute to recurrence even when they are no longer actively dividing. These surviving cells can continue producing and releasing a mixture of substances that influence the behavior of surrounding cells.

To investigate this process, Cole and his colleagues developed an experiment that separated the surviving cancer cells from the molecules they released. They discovered that these released substances, even without the surviving cells themselves, were enough to significantly increase cancer spread in a preclinical model.

"As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release -- not the cells themselves -- that drive the cancer's spread," stated Cole.

A Common Sugar Emerges as a Surprising Cancer Signal.

Industry observers note that the next challenge was identifying which substances were responsible for encouraging cancer cells to spread. The researchers discovered an unexpected culprit: fructose.

Recent findings suggest that fructose is a naturally occurring sugar found in fruit, honey, and other foods. It is also a component of table sugar and high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener frequently used in soft drinks and processed foods.

In a recent development, the study revealed that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy could produce fructose and release it into their surroundings. Rather than simply serving as an energy source, the sugar acted as a chemical messenger that encouraged neighboring cancer cells to become more capable of spreading.

The researchers also uncovered another concerning possibility. In their preclinical experiments, consuming high amounts of fructose comparable to those found in sugary drinks could promote signals associated with cancer spread even without chemotherapy treatment.

This observation suggests that diet might influence cancer progression through a mechanism scientists had not previously recognized. Fructose consumption is particularly relevant in the United States, where high fructose corn syrup can account for approximately 8% to 20% of daily calorie intake in some individuals.

Unlike many factors that influence cancer risk and progression, dietary fructose intake can be changed. That raises the possibility that nutritional strategies might eventually become part of efforts to limit cancer spread.

Sources indicate that however, researchers have not yet tested whether reducing fructose consumption improves outcomes in patients with ovarian cancer. The findings do not establish that eating sugar causes cancer to spread in humans, and additional research is needed before specific dietary recommendations can be made based on this mechanism.

How Fructose Helps Cancer Cells Break Free.

To understand how fructose encourages cancer spread, the researchers examined what happens inside cancer cells exposed to the sugar.

They used several advanced methods to investigate the biological changes involved, including a CRISPR screen. This technique allows scientists to systematically examine genes and identify which ones influence a particular cellular process.

The experiments revealed that fructose suppresses cholesterol production in neighboring cancer cells.

According to recent reports, although cholesterol is often discussed in connection with heart disease, it also serves essential functions throughout the body. It is an important component of cell membranes, the thin outer layers that surround cells and help regulate how they interact with their environment.

Recent findings suggest that in this case, cholesterol helps maintain the connections that hold neighboring cells together. These connections act somewhat like biological glue, making it harder for cancer cells to separate from one another.

Sources indicate that when fructose reduces cholesterol production, those connections weaken. As a result, cancer cells can detach more easily, potentially allowing them to escape and spread to other locations.

This discovery provides a possible explanation for how a common nutrient can influence one of the most dangerous aspects of cancer.

A Surprising Connection Between Statins and Cancer Spread.

The cholesterol finding also led researchers to investigate an unexpected question involving statins, medications widely prescribed to lower cholesterol.

In a recent development, approximately 39 million people in the United States take statins. These drugs work by reducing the body's production of cholesterol and are commonly used to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Because fructose appeared to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production, the research team wanted to know whether statins might produce similar effects.

Their experiments indicated that statins alone could weaken the connections between cancer cells, making it easier for them to separate and escape.

The finding raises questions about whether cholesterol-lowering medications could influence the effectiveness of chemotherapy in certain situations. Researchers are now investigating that possibility, but they emphasize that the results have not been demonstrated in patients and are not a reason for anyone to discontinue prescribed statins.

"We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," remarked Katherine Aird, Ph.D., professor and co-leader of the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program in the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center at The Wistar Institute, and senior author of the study.

Could Fructose Also Help Other Cancers Spread?

Although the research focused on ovarian cancer, the scientists suspect that the same biological process could occur in other forms of the disease.

Industry observers note that cancers affecting organs within the abdomen and torso can also spread to nearby tissues and organs. If fructose influences the connections between cancer cells in a similar way, the discovery could have implications beyond ovarian cancer.

According to recent reports, "We think other cancers that spread within the torso -- pancreatic, colon, liver -- could behave similarly. We can't call it universal yet, but we think the effects are not just limited to ovarian cancer," noted Aird.

Aird and Cole have already begun designing additional experiments to determine whether their findings can be reproduced in pancreatic, colon, liver, and other cancers.

According to recent reports, the research opens a fresh avenue for understanding how cancer spreads, particularly after chemotherapy. It also suggests that the relationship between nutrients, cholesterol production, and cancer cell behavior may be more complicated than previously understood.

While the potential implications for diet and medication remain uncertain, identifying fructose as a signal that helps cancer cells break free could eventually point researchers toward latest strategies for preventing metastasis and improving cancer treatment.

#44. Mangroves are making a comeback on the coast of Myanmar

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words)
General 🌐 Earth

Mangroves are making a comeback on the coast of Myanmar

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Landsat images reveal mangroves reclaiming former rice fields in Myanmar, offering a local view of a wider global forest recovery.
  • Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features a coastline where forests are reclaiming ground.
  • Along southern Myanmar, mangroves have spread into former rice fields and expanded beside waterways, adding green to places that looked noticeably more open 16 years earlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Landsat images reveal mangroves reclaiming former rice fields in Myanmar, offering a local view of a wider global forest recovery.

Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory features a coastline where forests are reclaiming ground.

Along southern Myanmar, mangroves have spread into former rice fields and expanded beside waterways, adding green to places that looked noticeably more open 16 years earlier.

The paired Landsat views capture part of Palaw Township in the country’s Myeik District. Brown agricultural patches interrupt the coastal vegetation in the earlier image.

In the later view, some of those patches have become greener as trees return.

According to recent reports, landsat 5’s Thematic Mapper recorded the first scene on February 14, 2010. Landsat 9’s Operational Land Imager captured the second on February 2, 2026.

Together, they offer a local view of a broader change: after decades of retreat, mangrove forests have begun gaining ground globally.

According to recent reports, south of the village of Kyauktaung, much of the apparent recovery occupies abandoned rice fields. Elsewhere along this coast, mangroves have spread into new areas.

Those two pathways matter. A forest can expand because trees return to land where they once grew, or because they establish themselves on newly available ground.

The resulting green patches may look similar from space, but they reflect different changes on the coast.

Nearby Pyin Bukyi Island has also been the setting for conservation and planting projects intended to support mangroves.

The images show a landscape where natural regeneration and human efforts can both contribute to recovery.

Myanmar’s recent gains follow substantial losses. Agriculture, aquaculture, and firewood harvesting removed mangroves across coastal areas during the 1980s and 1990s.

The country lost 28.6 percent of its mangrove area between the 1980s and 2010.

It has been revealed that since then, its mangrove area has increased by about 10 percent. That represents a reversal in direction, although it has not erased the earlier decline.

The local changes fit a global pattern identified by researchers who examined Landsat observations from 1984 through 2023.

Led by environmental scientist Zhen Zhang of Tulane University, the team tracked both mangrove extent and canopy cover.

Their study, published in the journal Science, found that the global balance shifted from net loss to net gain around 2010.

Sources indicate that between 1984 and 2010, mangroves lost nearly 3,000 square kilometers, or 1,200 square miles. After 2010, they gained nearly 2,000 square kilometers, or 770 square miles.

The researchers also found increasing canopy cover in forests that persisted through the study period.

That distinction adds another dimension to the recovery: some existing forests were filling in as mangroves expanded elsewhere.

By 2023, global mangrove extent was approximately 0.5 percent below its level in the 1980s, with uncertainty around that estimate.

Much of the earlier loss had therefore been offset, although the global total conceals substantial differences among regions.

In a recent development, mangroves occupy a shifting boundary between land and sea. In some places, rivers deliver enough sediment to build mudflats where trees can take root.

Sediment accumulation has helped mangroves expand around the Amazon River’s mouth and across parts of northern Australia. These coastal changes have supported gains there since the 1990s.

Temperature also influences where mangroves can grow.

Along the colder edges of their range, including the southeastern United States, warmer conditions and fewer freezes have allowed trees to establish themselves in previously unsuitable areas.

Globally, about two-thirds of the expansion identified by the researchers came from mangroves colonizing new areas.

Restoration and regrowth in degraded places accounted for the remaining third.

The findings show why a mangrove comeback cannot be measured simply by counting planted trees.

Natural expansion and the return of forests to previously cleared land account for much of the change.

Mangroves help protect shorelines from erosion and storm surges.

Their roots shelter fish, shrimp, crabs, and other marine animals, while the ecosystems store substantial amounts of carbon.

Sources indicate that those benefits make the returning forests significant for coastal communities as well as wildlife. But recovery remains uneven.

Losses in the Niger Delta have contributed to declining mangrove area across West and Central Africa since 2010.

Tropical cyclones have also degraded extensive forests in North America and southern Africa.

In a recent development, the Myanmar images capture one encouraging part of that complicated picture. Fields have given way to trees, and stretches of coast have gained forest cover.

The larger challenge is keeping that recovery going while protecting the mangroves that remain.

#41. Tech Report: The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words)
General 🌐 Sciencenews

Tech Report: The brain’s fear center moonlights as the save button for memories

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read | Source: Sciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every print subscription comes with full digital access.
  • Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered.
  • The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access.

Amygdala neurons activated when people viewed images they later remembered.

The amygdala, highlighted in orange, is responsible for regulating emotions like fear and aggression. A latest study also reveals its role sorting memories for longer term storage.

KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The walnut-sized fear center of the brain also distinguishes the memorable from the mundane.

Sources indicate that neurons in the amygdala act like a save button for memories, scientists report October 27 in Nature Neuroscience. Though the study doesn’t nail down the exact mechanism for memory formation, it points to a broader role for the amygdala within the memory-sorting apparatus.

It has been revealed that the study probes an enduring quandary about the mind, says neuroscientist Jiayang Xiao of Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University in Los Angeles. “We forget much of what we experience … only a fraction of the information we encounter becomes a lasting memory,” she says.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Although a role for the amygdala in memory has been suggested before, previous studies that used electrodes reading brain activity through the scalp, or at the scale of thousands rather than individual neurons, captured a blurrier picture. It’s akin to a microphone recording from outside of a stadium, indicates cognitive neuroscientist Cory Inman at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who was not involved in the study.

“You might be able to tell that there’s a game happening. You might be able to tell when somebody scores a touchdown. You might even be able to tell that one side of the stadium is cheering for one team and another side of the stadium is cheering for another team,” but that’s about it, Inman states. The new study is more like a lapel mic pinned on a single fan in terms of scale and what the researchers were able to capture, adding clarity.

The amygdala, which is typically associated with regulating emotions like fear and aggression, has neurons that are challenging to reach, residing in two clusters deep within the brain. Xiao and her colleagues leveraged electrodes previously surgically implanted in more than 90 people with drug-resistant epilepsy to identify where seizures originate. In their newly introduced role, the electrodes singled out neurons involved in saving memories.

Patients were shown images of everyday objects belonging to five categories such as food and animals. About 10 to 30 minutes later, they attempted to recall which images were already shown. Xiao and her colleagues found that activity in certain amygdala neurons corresponded with an image being remembered. The image had been earmarked for longer term storage, Xiao indicates.

It has been revealed that although participants had to recall something from half an hour ago at most and the exact mechanism for saving memories is still unclear, the researchers think there are two main steps of the process. The team highlighted that individual neurons have a preference for one of the five categories of images. First the image is categorized by the amygdala. Then, the strength of the category neuron response the first time the image is shown dictates whether the image is later recalled.

A better understanding of this mechanism may pave the way for more effective treatments of memory disorders, Xiao says, a medical conundrum for which there are presently no broadly effective treatments.

Recent findings suggest that the hippocampus is typically more directly linked to memory, so “it surprised me that we observe such a clear relationship between memory formation and activity in the amygdala,” Xiao says. By contrast, the correlation between hippocampus neuron activity and image recall was weaker and slightly delayed.

Future work like observing the impacts of stimulating amygdala neurons on memory will help researchers discern if this region can be targeted to improve memory, Xiao indicates.

For now, the secret to memory’s hidden machinations remains in the shadows.

#40. Breaking: America’s power grid is falling behind as electricity demand surges

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6 min read (1119 words)
General 🌐 Earth

Breaking: America’s power grid is falling behind as electricity demand surges

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • America’s electricity demand is rising, but power line construction is lagging.
  • It has been revealed that electricity demand in the United States is rising fast.
  • It has been revealed that technology that can move far greater amounts of power already exists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

America’s electricity demand is rising, but power line construction is lagging. A new analysis examines the barriers and possible solutions.

It has been revealed that electricity demand in the United States is rising fast. However, the high-voltage lines needed to carry that power between regions are not being built at anything like the rate required.

It has been revealed that technology that can move far greater amounts of power already exists. A fresh analysis by energy policy experts links the shortfall to something else, namely the way decisions about power lines get made.

The analysis was written by Madeline Yozwiak and M. Granger Morgan of Carnegie Mellon University and David G. Victor of the University of California San Diego.

It is a policy paper (not an experiment) that draws upon earlier studies and reports.

Recent findings suggest that few places, the authors wrote, face as extreme a shortage as the United States. “The fundamental challenge isn’t technical, it’s jurisdictional,” the authors wrote.

In a recent development, “Authority is divided among federal, state, and private entities, each with distinct priorities. When every stakeholder possesses the power to say no, even high-value projects that benefit the entire nation struggle to move forward.”.

Across the continental United States, only about 500 miles per year of new high-voltage lines (345 kilovolts or above) have been built in the past five years.

The figure is just a tenth of the 5,000 upcoming miles per year that studies suggest will be needed, the authors wrote, citing a Department of Energy report.

At the higher rate, the grid that links regions would triple by 2050.

Demand is rising partly because of electric vehicles, electrified heavy industry, and the rapid growth of data centers.

Wind and solar power are also variable, which means that a grid depending on it has to move more power over longer distances.

Mileage is only part of the problem, however.

Where the lines are built matters too, the authors wrote, since links between whole regions can make the power grid more reliable and lower consumer costs.

History is part of the reason. Before the 1920s, electric power was mainly a local and regional business.

States granted each utility the sole right to serve its area, and in return a state commission was given control of its prices.

The federal government played only a secondary role until the energy crisis of the 1970s, when a stronger regulator, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), was created.

FERC gradually gained authority over line planning and rates, but key elements of state oversight were left intact.

Regulated utilities own most of the transmission lines, and state regulators reward them for projects built inside their own territories.

A line that crosses state borders involves more players, triggers federal oversight, and raises arguments about which customers pay.

A utility that owns both power plants and lines can profit when limited transmission keeps prices high.

According to recent reports, independent developers aren’t tied to one territory. Even so, laws in 10 states give the existing utility first claim on a proposed project.

There are two upgrades that can add capacity without a latest route.

The wires on an existing high-voltage line can be replaced, or the line can be converted to direct current (DC), and either can sometimes triple its capacity.

These upgrades use existing routes, where local opposition may be weaker because power lines are already in place.

Recent findings suggest that alternating current, used on most of the grid, can only be moved over short distances when the cable is buried. DC cables, however, can run underground much farther.

One example is the Champlain Hudson Power Express, a 339-mile (545-kilometer) line that was built to carry hydropower from Quebec to Fresh York City.

Its cables are buried along transportation corridors and under Lake Champlain and the Hudson River.

Illinois bans new lines along highways and railroads, whereas laws have been passed in Michigan and Wisconsin to make such projects easier.

The authors made three proposals, and the first needs no fresh laws.

Under a 2005 law, the Department of Energy is allowed to name corridors of national interest, where the permitting of new power lines is simpler.

In 2021 the program was relaunched, but the corridors that had been named were canceled by the Trump administration in August 2026.

The authors called the framework solid and urged the federal agencies to create several such corridors again.

There is a role for the states as well. The laws that give existing utilities the first claim on fresh projects could be repealed.

In addition, more of a line’s benefits could be shared with host communities, which would reward building rather than blocking.

Texas took this approach with its Competitive Renewable Energy Zone program, in which proposals sought directly from stakeholders created a race to build.

Other nations face similar challenges, the authors wrote.

Sweden, which is rich in hydropower, rejected a link with Germany because it feared higher power prices at home.

France and Spain needed six years to reach a cost-sharing deal for an undersea link.

As a partial fix, the European Union and Australia have created joint processes for planning and building lines across member countries and states.

Industry observers note that the second proposal is to learn from this experience. A cross-national forum, led by the national association of state utility regulators, would study what has worked abroad.

Existing comparisons of power grids, the authors wrote, tend to be too broad for lessons to move from one place to another.

Sources indicate that the third proposal is a Presidential-Congressional Transmission Commission. It would be created by Congress together with the White House.

Recent findings suggest that what would such a commission do? It would draft laws at the federal and state levels, assess whether the powers of FERC or other bodies should be expanded, and identify which incentives deserve public money.

However, public spending won’t be the main answer in a time of tightening budgets, the authors wrote.

Instead, bonus incentives (such as money and faster permits) could be offered to the developers who build first and to the communities that host their lines.

Private investors will ultimately decide what gets built, the authors wrote, and there will be no single national plan.

The authors did not estimate how much additional transmission construction these incentives would encourage. The commission itself remains only a proposal.

A bipartisan federal bill was also proposed recently that would, if adopted, ease permitting and reduce delays and veto points, the authors suggest.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#39. Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7 min read (1435 words)
General 🌐 Sciencedaily

Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when muscles are injured, the body normally activates specialized stem cells that help rebuild damaged tissue.
  • Researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania have identified an unexpected role for a protein called TRF2, which was previously known primarily for protecting chromosomes.
  • The discovery, published in Science Advances, could provide newly introduced directions for muscular dystrophy treatments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when muscles are injured, the body normally activates specialized stem cells that help rebuild damaged tissue. But scientists have discovered that without one critical protein, this repair system can break down, leaving injured muscles filled with fat and scar tissue instead of healthy muscle.

Researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania have identified an unexpected role for a protein called TRF2, which was previously known primarily for protecting chromosomes. Their findings suggest that TRF2 is also essential for maintaining the identity of muscle stem cells, allowing them to continue repairing and regenerating muscle throughout life.

The discovery, published in Science Advances, could provide newly introduced directions for muscular dystrophy treatments. It may also help scientists understand vital differences between muscle regeneration and cancer, including why skeletal muscle can repair itself so effectively while cancers originating in muscle are relatively uncommon.

Industry observers note that "For years, TRF2 has been viewed as a protein whose primary job is protecting the ends of chromosomes from damage or corruption," mentioned senior author Foteini Mourkioti, PhD, an associate professor of Orthopedic Surgery at Penn Medicine. "But rather than simply protecting DNA, TRF2 seems to be key to regenerating muscle throughout life.".

A Hidden Protein With an Unexpected Role in Muscle Repair.

In a recent development, for years, scientists have studied TRF2 because of its role in safeguarding telomeres, the protective structures found at the ends of chromosomes. Chromosomes carry our genetic information, and telomeres help keep their ends from deteriorating or being mistaken for damaged DNA.

The new research demonstrates that TRF2 has another notable responsibility. It helps muscle stem cells retain the genetic instructions that make them muscle stem cells in the first place. Maintaining that identity is essential because these specialized cells serve as the body's reserve supply for repairing injured muscle.

Under normal conditions, muscle stem cells spend much of their time inactive. When an injury occurs, they become active, multiply, and help replace damaged muscle tissue. Some then return to a resting state, preserving a population of stem cells that can respond to future injuries.

Recent findings suggest that through laboratory experiments, the researchers found that TRF2 levels change as muscle stem cells move between these different stages. The protein's activity rises and falls as the cells transition from dormancy to repair and then replenish themselves, suggesting that TRF2 helps regulate the entire regeneration process.

Without TRF2, Damaged Muscles Accumulate Fat and Scar Tissue.

It has been revealed that to understand how important TRF2 is, the scientists removed the protein from muscle stem cells in laboratory mice. At first, the animals' muscles appeared normal, suggesting that the loss of TRF2 did not immediately damage existing muscle tissue.

Industry observers note that over time, however, a serious problem emerged. The population of functional muscle stem cells began to decline, leaving the animals increasingly unable to repair damaged muscle.

Sources indicate that the researchers initially expected the cells to die, since losing TRF2 can produce that outcome in other tissues. Instead, they discovered something more surprising: the cells remained alive but lost the molecular identity that allowed them to function as muscle stem cells.

In effect, the cells no longer maintained the biological program needed to perform their specialized repair duties.

The consequences became clear when the muscles were injured. Rather than rebuilding healthy muscle, the damaged tissue accumulated fat and scar tissue, a form of tissue replacement that cannot restore normal muscle function.

In a recent development, "This completely changes how we think about TRF2's role in these cells," stated Mourkioti. "The loss of identity has severe implications for whether recovery from injury is even possible.".

A Potential Breakthrough for Muscular Dystrophy Research.

The team also investigated whether TRF2 plays a role in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a serious inherited disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness and degeneration. The disease interferes with the body's ability to maintain healthy muscles, making effective repair especially notable.

Using a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the researchers removed TRF2 from muscle stem cells and observed a dramatic worsening of the disease.

According to recent reports, muscle degeneration progressed much faster, and the affected mice had shorter survival times. These findings indicate that TRF2 plays an crucial role in preserving the regenerative capacity of muscles already struggling with a serious genetic disease.

The results do not yet establish a latest treatment for muscular dystrophy. However, they identify a biological mechanism that researchers may eventually be able to target to help preserve muscle stem cell function and improve tissue repair.

How TRF2 Protects the Identity of Muscle Stem Cells.

Further experiments revealed how TRF2 performs this unexpected function.

Although the protein is best known for working at the ends of chromosomes, the researchers found that it also attaches to regulatory regions throughout the genome. These regions help control which genes are active or inactive, determining how cells behave and what specialized functions they perform.

According to recent reports, for muscle stem cells, this regulation is particularly crucial. Their ability to repair muscle depends on maintaining a specific pattern of gene activity that preserves their identity and regenerative potential.

According to recent reports, the scientists discovered that many of the DNA regions associated with TRF2 contain unusual structures known as G-quadruplexes. These structures form when sections of DNA rich in the building block guanine fold into distinctive arrangements involving four interacting strands or segments.

G-quadruplexes have attracted considerable scientific interest because they can influence how genes function. They are also being investigated as possible targets for cancer treatments.

The Penn researchers found that TRF2 interacts with these specialized DNA structures to help maintain the genetic program that keeps muscle stem cells functioning properly.

"We found that TRF2 works through these secondary DNA structures to preserve the identity of muscle stem cells and keep them capable of repairing damaged muscle," Mourkioti said. "That was completely unexpected.".

What Muscle Regeneration Could Reveal About Cancer.

Beyond muscular dystrophy, the discovery may help researchers investigate a longstanding mystery about muscle biology.

Skeletal muscle, the type of muscle that allows the body to move, has an impressive ability to regenerate after injury. Yet cancers that originate in skeletal muscle are relatively rare, even though other tissues with substantial regenerative activity can be more vulnerable to cancer.

This raises an crucial question: how can muscle maintain such a powerful repair system without frequently developing cancer?

The researchers believe that TRF2's unusual role in muscle stem cells could offer clues. By examining how the protein regulates gene activity in muscle compared with other tissues, scientists may gain a better understanding of the mechanisms that support regeneration while limiting the risk of uncontrolled cell growth.

That distinction matters because cancer develops when cells acquire changes that allow them to grow and divide without the normal biological restraints. Finding ways to strengthen muscle repair without encouraging abnormal growth would be an important goal for future therapies.

In a recent development, mourkioti and her colleagues are now investigating whether the way muscle stem cells use TRF2 could lead to new treatment strategies for muscular dystrophy. They also hope to determine what this mechanism can reveal about cancer biology in tissues that are more susceptible to the disease.

According to recent reports, although additional research is needed to determine whether these findings can be translated into treatments for people, the discovery reveals an key part of the body's muscle repair system. It also demonstrates that a protein long associated with protecting DNA has a much broader role in keeping muscles capable of healing.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health/ National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (R01 DK123356, R01s CA174904, GM101149, and FDN-143330).

According to recent reports, when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It has been revealed that STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours.

Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines.

According to recent reports, the flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch. Following stage separation, Super Heavy reoriented for a planned return to Starbase as Ship powered its way toward low Earth orbit (LEO).

SpaceX originally planned to catch Super Heavy with the Starbase launch tower's giant mechanical "chopstick" arms. But it wasn't to be: The manufacturer called off the catch attempt and brought the booster down for a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico about 6.5 minutes after launch, for reasons that were not immediately clear.

A successful catch would have been a significant milestone for SpaceX and its efforts to design Starship as a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle. It would have been the first successful recovery of a Version 3 (V3) Super Heavy, which SpaceX began flying earlier this year. The firm previously recovered three of its V1 Super Heavy vehicles and reused two of those in later flights.

Ship's Raptors continued to fire following stage separation, completing their first burn just after eight minutes into flight. All went according to blueprint after that for Ship as well: A second engine burn lasting about 20 seconds parked Ship in LEO at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) at T+26 minutes and 10 seconds.

It has been revealed that "We’ve got a nominal orbit insertion, so Starship now in orbit around Earth for the second time ever," SpaceX's Dan Huot said during today's Flight 15 launch webcast. "That’s a really great moment.".

Ship first reached orbit on Flight 14, which debuted on Sept. 28.

Ship carried 26 of SpaceX's Starlink V3 spacecraft, which were deployed into LEO on schedule today over a 42-minute span starting 35 minutes after launch.

The upgraded wireless internet satellites are the second V3 batch to reach orbit, after a set of 26 that were delivered on Flight 14 . V3s are significantly more powerful than SpaceX's V2 Starlinks, which right now number more than 11,000 in LEO. The addition of this newly introduced set of V3s will add a terabit of data capacity to the constellation, according to SpaceX's Flight 15 mission outline. That's equivalent to the amount contributed by 10 Starlink V2 introduces, which are carried out by SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket.

Industry observers note that three of the V3 Starlinks flying today were equipped with cameras to point back at Ship after deployment in order to analyze its heatshield tiles and other hardware following its ascent to orbit. Their data will help SpaceX determine if Ship can indeed come home to Starbase on Saturday.

"Starship will only execute a return to launch site if the flight control team has ensured that the vehicle systems critical for reentry maneuvers and final landing burn and tower approach are healthy," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description.

SpaceX engineers will have ample time to go over Ship's systems before making a final landing decision. Ship is scheduled to circle Earth 14 times, spending more than 21 hours in space before coming home.

You can follow all of the action on here at Space.com via our Flight 15 live updates page.

It has been revealed that spaceX has reserved three contingency checkpoints during Flight 15's mission timeline to allow for an early Pacific Ocean return, should engineers determine a catch attempt to be unfeasible or unwise. The first comes just 10 minutes after the completion of Starlink satellite deployment, the second at T+7 hours and 15 minutes, and a final one at T+20 hours and 41 minutes.

Should Ship continue to look good through each of these milestones, SpaceX will proceed with a 10-second deorbit burn at approximately T+21 hours and 36 minutes, setting the spacecraft on a trajectory back toward South Texas. Its plunge through Earth's atmosphere will begin about 35 minutes later. SpaceX has also designated a contingency splashdown zone in the Gulf of Mexico, should conditions prevent a safe catch during Ship's final approach.

If all goes according to strategy, Ship will return to Starbase on Saturday at approximately 4:17 p.m. EST (2117 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Texas time), about 22.5 hours after liftoff. A successful catch would be a major milestone for SpaceX — the first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage.

According to recent reports, full reusability is central to the manufacturer's ambitions for launching its V3 Starlink satellites, as well as a proposed constellation of orbital data centers envisioned by company founder and CEO Elon Musk. The next-gen Starlink constellation will consist of about 100,000 satellites, while the AI network will be 10 times that size, Musk has noted. Building and maintaining those constellations will require a mind-boggling number of launches. Indeed, SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship liftoffs per year by 2030, according to Musk.

Some of Starship's other planned missions won't necessarily require full reusability, but the spacecraft's reliability will be critical to NASA's Artemis program and its efforts to return astronauts to the moon. The space agency selected Starship as one of the program's crewed lunar landers, and it's slated to fly a demonstration mission with NASA's Orion spacecraft and Artemis III astronauts to Earth orbit in the summer of 2027.

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Industry observers note that celebrate Friday the 13th with something spooky: a ghost in the constellation Andromeda. This evening, point your telescope toward 2nd-magnitude Mirach (Beta [β] Andromedae), already nearly 60° high in the east by 7 P.M. local time. One of the Princess’ brightest stars, Mirach is a cool, reddish M-type giant. It lies some 200 light-years away and shines nearly 2,000 times as brightly as our Sun.

But Mirach is not quite our target — we’re looking for its so-called ghost, just 6.8’ northwest of the star. You’ll need a significant scope to see it, but look carefully: Can you spot a faint smudge of light, about 4’ across, close to the star? This is the Ghost of Mirach, a far more distant elliptical galaxy glowing at 10th magnitude and cataloged as NGC 404. It lies some 8 million to 10 million light-years away, just beyond the gravitational bounds of our Local Group of galaxies. It’s called a ghost because it appears almost like a ghostly image of the bright star Mirach, which dominates the view.

#35. Industry News: Teenage boys are spending less time outside, but what has changed?

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5 min read (1036 words)
General 🌐 Earth

Industry News: Teenage boys are spending less time outside, but what has changed?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read | Source: Earth

💡 Key Takeaways
  • teenage boys’ outdoor time fell from over an hour a day around 2010 to under 40 minutes by 2023, while girls’ outdoor time changed little.
  • According to recent reports, teenage boys in the United States once spent considerably more time outdoors than teenage girls.
  • American boys aged 15 to 19 averaged more than 60 minutes a day outdoors around 2010.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, U.S. teenage boys’ outdoor time fell from over an hour a day around 2010 to under 40 minutes by 2023, while girls’ outdoor time changed little.

According to recent reports, teenage boys in the United States once spent considerably more time outdoors than teenage girls. Around 2010, that gap was still clear. Since then, boys’ outdoor time has fallen sharply.

American boys aged 15 to 19 averaged more than 60 minutes a day outdoors around 2010. By 2023 they were under 40 minutes.

According to recent reports, girls initially spent less time outdoors, and their average changed little. By 2023, boys and girls were spending similarly limited amounts of time outside.

The analysis was led by Ewa Jarosz in the Department of Psychology at the University of Oslo.

Her co-authors were Vidar Ulset of the Norwegian School of Sport Sciences and Vegard Skirbekk, who also works at the Norwegian Institute of Public Health.

Time outdoors is where teenagers get their daylight and a large share of their physical activity, and the study can’t say what caused the drop, only what moved alongside it.

The numbers come from the American Time Use Survey, which the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has run since 2003.

Each person in it walks an interviewer through one full day, activity by activity, with where they were and who was with them.

The team pulled every diary from someone aged 15 to 19 between 2003 and 2023, which came to 14,235 days.

Time counted as outdoors when the diary placed the person outside away from home, or walking or cycling somewhere.

It also counted when the activity only happens outside, such as mowing a lawn, hunting or playing an outdoor sport.

Industry observers note that some outdoor time was missed on purpose. The survey lumps home and yard together, and it doesn’t say whether time at school was in a classroom or on a field, so neither was counted.

The team applied the same rule to every year, allowing consistent comparisons while leaving some outdoor time unmeasured.

Outdoor time for all teenagers fell over the 20 years, and the decline was concentrated among boys.

Girls’ time changed little, and the sex difference that was clear in 2010 was no longer detectable in recent years.

The steepest part of the drop for boys came after the pandemic, in both whether they went out at all and how long they stayed.

The year 2020 itself was left out of the trend lines because the survey was disrupted that year.

Some things went with more outdoor time for both sexes.

Teenagers under 16 spent more time outside than older ones, as did those in the Northeast and West and those from higher-income households.

Weekends brought longer stretches outside. Black teenagers were more likely to go out on a given day but stayed out for less time.

The team then set outdoor time beside three other ways of spending leisure: computer use and gaming, indoor exercise, and time with friends.

Smartphones were left out, because the survey didn’t measure them the same way every year and because a phone can be used outside.

Boys in the top quarter for computer leisure were less likely to go outside at all, and spent less time there when they did.

Girls showed a similar pattern, but the association was not statistically significant.

Boys who were heavy computer users spent about as much time outdoors as girls.

According to recent reports, time with friends ran the other way. Teenagers who spent more than the typical amount of time with a friend were more likely to be outside, boys and girls alike.

It has been revealed that the quarter who spent the most time with friends also stayed out longest. Over the same 20 years, time with friends fell sharply for both.

It has been revealed that in an interview with Earth.com, Jarosz said hanging out itself is in decline. It used to be low-cost and easy to arrange, she said, and now “it is crowded out by other activities.”.

Could more indoor exercise have offset the loss of outdoor time? The study found no increase in indoor physical activity over the period.

Teenagers who exercised indoors were also more likely to spend time outdoors.

One kind of activity went with the other rather than replacing it.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most, Jarosz mentioned the decline among boys, which worries her.

Men need more physical activity than women to get the same heart benefits, she remarked.

Jarosz suggested that less outdoor time could also leave boys fewer opportunities for rough-and-tumble play.

The researchers noted that indoor exercise is also selective, with cost a common barrier, and that a recent pooled analysis found people enjoy it less than activity outdoors.

Each teenager appears once, on one day, so the study tracks a population rather than following any person as they grow.

The diaries also say nothing about what the outdoors looked like, so a wooded park and a parking lot count the same.

Asked what parents can do, Jarosz said habits are mostly set earlier in childhood, and that for 15- to 19-year-olds the peer group matters more than parents do.

Recent findings suggest that she was careful to call that her view rather than a study finding. She pointed instead at where teenagers live.

“We know this is highly stratified, which means that it depends on your socioeconomic status what type of outdoor environment you have nearby,” Jarosz noted.

Whether the decline has bottomed out is an open question. Jarosz noted outdoor time ticked up slightly in 2021 compared with 2020, by too little to count, and that she expects some recovery now that the pandemic is over.

“The decline started already around 2010 and I think the likelihood of returning to 2010 levels of outdoor time without some intervention is probably low,” she told Earth.com.

The next diaries will show whether she is right, one day at a time.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

It has been revealed that the Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

According to recent reports, when you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

Sources indicate that the U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

Sources indicate that "When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

In a recent development, it takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

In a recent development, experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

Industry observers note that the nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in Newly introduced York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

According to recent reports, in the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.
